title: Greek Anthology
text:
1. Philippus
A single pentameter
Hail, Paphian goddess: for your power is everlasting,
your deathless beauty and your honoured awe—
all mortal men, the creatures of a day,
revere you in their every word and every noble deed;
for everywhere, to all alike, you show your honour clear.
2. Phaedimus
A trimeter
Callistratus, the youth of Cephisia,
set up for you, O messenger of Zeus,
this likeness shared with one of his own age:
delight in it, and keep Apollodorus' son and city safe.
3. Theocritus
A limping trimeter
Here lies the poet Hipponax.
If you are base, do not draw near the tomb;
but if you are honest, of decent stock,
sit down and take your ease, and sleep if you will.
4. Anacreon
A tetrameter
You, Aristocleides, of all my friends I pity first:
you lost your youth defending your homeland from slavery.
5. Phalaecus
A curtailed or docked trimeter
"I win the double course." "But I am a wrestler."
"And I the pentathlon." "But I am a boxer." —
"And who are you?" "Timodemus." "But I am a Cretan."
"And I am Cretheus." "But I am Diocles." —
"And who is your father?" "Cleinus." "As mine is too." — "And where do you win?" "At the Isthmus." "And you?" —
"In the Nemean meadow, and at Hera's shrine."
6. Phalaecus
The eleven-syllable trimeter, so called
This portrait, the surpassing image
of the man who made the world laugh in comedy,
crowned for his triumph with ivy and with garlands,
I have set up, that it may mark Lycon's grave.
For all that he was once a shining man . . .
a memorial of that man of charm, in the gathering-place
and over the wine, this stands for those who come after,
a token left behind, an image of his face.
7. Callimachus
A comic tetrameter
Menoetas of Lyctus dedicated this bow,
saying as he laid it down: "Here, I give you the horn and the quiver,
Sarapis; the Hesperitae keep the arrows."
8. Theodoridas
The Hesperitae.
An Archilochian tetrameter
This hammered cauldron of bronze, won by his speed in the long race,
the son of Aristomachus carried off as his prize.
9. Callimachus
A bacchic pentameter. The epigram is not complete.
Many an amphora comes cleaving the Aegean from the vineyards of Chios,
and many a one bringing the choice nectar of the Lesbian vine.
10. Callimachus
A tetrameter of sixteen syllables. This too is incomplete.
O ship, that snatched from me the one sweet light of my life,
I beg you, by Zeus the watcher of the harbour . . .
11. Simonides
A pentameter for the dance
A. Who set up this statue? B. Dorieus of Thurii.
A. Was he not Rhodian by birth? B. Yes, before he fled his homeland,
having done with terrible hand many deeds of violence.
12. Hegesippus
A trimeter sung in answer to a hexameter
Cursed be that day, and the deadly dark,
and the dread roaring of the wind-tossed sea,
that once overturned the ship on which that man, so sweet of soul,
prayed in vain to the gods for the Abderites;
for it was wrecked through all, and driven by the surge
upon rough Seriphus, where, granted fire
by the hands of reverent hosts, he came at last to his homeland,
Abdera, his ashes wrapped in an urn of bronze.
13. Anonymous epigrammatists
A pentameter upon a hexameter, then a trimeter
Pyres, the dear son of Polymnestus, dedicated this,
having vowed a tithe to Pallas Tritogeneia;
Cresilas of Cydonia wrought it.
14. Simonides
A pentameter upon a hexameter and two trimeters, then a hexameter
Here lies Dandes of Argos, runner of the stadium,
who brought glory to his horse-pasturing homeland with his victories—
twice at Olympia, three times at Pytho,

title: Greek Anthology
text:
twice at the Isthmus, fifteen times at Nemea;
and his other victories it is not easy to count.
15. Anonymous epigrammatists
A pentameter upon two hexameters
I am Dicon, son of Callimbrotus; and I won
four times at Nemea, twice at Olympia, five times at Pytho,
three times at the Isthmus; I crown the city of Syracuse.
16. Anonymous epigrammatists
A pentameter upon three hexameters.
Kings of Sparta were my fathers and my brothers;
and I, Cynisca, victorious with my chariot of swift-footed horses,
set up this statue. I declare that I alone of women
in all Greece have won this crown.
17. Anonymous epigrammatists
A dimeter upon a hexameter
Iphion painted this with his own hand,
he whom the water of Pirene once nourished.
18. Parmeniscus
An eleven-syllable line upon a hexameter
Works of bronze, proclaim the victory of the swift filly,
who, goaded into a charge, threw off her rider
and, riderless, raced over the level course. From that time on
Parmenon won the golden victory.
Phocritus, to your son the Amyclean kings
granted to win the prizes of his fathers.
19. Simonides
A nine-syllable line upon a hexameter
Nicoladas of Corinth, who won the victory
at Delphi in the foot-race, dedicated this offering,
and at the Panathenaea took five crowns in the contests,
amphorae of oil one after another;
at the holy Isthmus three times in a row
the shore of the Lord of the Sea knew him take the prize;
three times he won at Nemea, and four more times
at Pellene, twice in the Lycaean games,
and at Tegea, and at Aegina, and at mighty Epidaurus,
and at Thebes, and among the people of Megara;
and in the stadium at Phlius, winning all five events,
he gladdened the heart of great Corinth.
20. Simonides
Upon a hexameter, alternating, the comic tetrameter short by two
syllables and the limping Archilochian trimeter
Glorifying his homeland, the holy city of Athena's people,
Opis, child of the dark earth, fashioned these lovely pipes
together with Hephaestus, and dedicated them to Aphrodite,
mastered by his longing for the lovely Bryson.
21. Theodoridas
Upon the regular trimeter a dimeter taken from the dance pentameter
This is the tomb of Mnasalces of Plataea,
the maker of elegies;
and his Muse was a torn-off fragment
of Simonides' broad style—
empty in its clamour, a flask-thumping bawler of dithyrambs.
He is dead—let us not throw at him; but if he lived,
he would be banging on his drum.
22. Phaedimus
Upon the regular trimeter a heroic tetrameter as refrain, limping at the next-to-last
The bow with which you slew the Giant's strength,
restrain its force, far-shooting lord:
. . . his wolf-slaying quiver is not unloosed;
but turn upon these young men an arrow
of Eros, that they may defend their homeland,
made bold by their love of youths;
for it kindles valour, and this, the highest of the gods,
ever exalts the champions in the front.
And you, ancestral glory of the men of Schoenus,
receive the grateful offering of Melistion.
23. Asclepiades
Upon the tetrameter formed from a regular trimeter by the addition of a final foot, a curtailed trimeter
O passer-by, even if you are in some haste, stop a moment, I beg you, and hear
how great, indeed, was the sorrow of Botrys,
who, an old man of eighty years, buried his son of nine,
a child already wise and skilled in speech.
Alas for the father, and alas for you too, dear child of Botrys,
bereft of how many pleasures you have perished.
24. Callimachus
An eleven-syllable line upon the last metron of the foregoing tetrameter
The gifts to Aphrodite.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
Simon, the wanderer, dedicated her own image,
and the girdle
that loved her breasts, and the torch,
and the thyrsi she once tossed aloft,
shrieking, poor woman, up among the hills.
25. Callimachus
Upon the doubled metron, an epodic tetrameter, exceeding the hexameter by one syllable
To Demeter of the Gates, for whom Acrisius
once built this temple, not the Pelasgian one, these gifts
did Timodemus of Naucratis set up,
and to her daughter below—a tithe of his gains; for so he vowed.
26. Simonides
Upon the same tetrameter, a curtailed trimeter
I will remember; for it is not fitting that the radiant wife
of Archenautes should lie here nameless in death,
Xanthippe, descendant of Periander, who once
gave law to the people, holding the high-towered bounds of Corinth.
27. Phalaecus
Upon the tetrameter a regular trimeter, then a hexameter alternating
Phocus perished in a foreign land; for the black ship
did not bear him up above the wave, nor receive him,
but down into the deep gulf of the Aegean sea he sank,
when the South Wind drove its violence over the farthest deep.
He won a share of an empty tomb among his fathers, around which Promethis,
his mother, like a mournful bird in her fate,
cries "Alas!" for her own child all her days,
telling how, before his time, he perished.
27a. Callimachus
Upon the same tetrameter, an eleven-syllable line
. . .
28. Simonides
Upon the same tetrameter, a tetrameter like "if only a maiden fair and tender were mine," exceeding by one syllable alone; in the fourth foot it has not an iamb but an anapaest
Often, indeed, in the dances of the Acamantid tribe the Seasons
have raised the cry over the ivy-crowned dithyrambs,
the daughters of Dionysus, and with fillets and the choicest roses
they shaded the glistening hair of the skilled singers,
who set up this tripod for themselves, a witness of the Bacchic contests;
and it was Antigenes who trained those men.
Well did Ariston of Argos nurse the sweet voice for the Dorian strains,
pouring his sweet breath purely through the pipes;
and Hipponicus, son of Struthon, furnished the choir
of honey-voiced singers, borne in the chariot of the Graces,
who set upon him among men a glorious name and shining victory,
by the will of the violet-crowned goddesses, the Muses.
29. Nicaenetus
Upon a hexameter, a trimeter
Wine is a swift horse to the graceful singer;
but drinking water you would bring forth nothing wise.
This Cratinus said, Dionysus, and he breathed the fragrance
not of one wineskin, but reeked of a whole great jar.
And so he flourished mightily under the garlands, and his brow
was wreathed with ivy, as is yours, in saffron decked.
30. Simonides
This too is a hexameter and a trochaic tetrameter by transposition
of the words
Muse, sing to me the son of fair-ankled Alcmena.
The son of Alcmena sing to me, Muse, of the fair ankles.
31. Timocreon
Likewise
The folly of Ceos came upon me against my will.
Against my will the folly of Ceos came upon me.
1. Socrates
Polycrates:
Blessed Pythagoras, Heliconian scion of the Muses,
tell me, since I ask: how many in the contest of wisdom
are in your halls, contending nobly for the prize?
Pythagoras:
I will tell you, then, Polycrates. Half of them
press on toward the fair branches of learning; a fourth
labour over the nature of the immortal; a seventh
are wholly given to silence, and to imperishable inward words;
three are women, and Theano excels the rest.
So many ministers of the Muses I myself lead on.
2. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a statue of Pallas
Golden Pallas am I, of beaten gold; and the gold

title: Greek Anthology
text:
is the gift of vigorous men, the followers of song.
Half the gold Charisius gave, and an eighth part
Thespis, and a tenth part Solon gave,
a twentieth Themison; and the remaining talents,
nine of them, and the workmanship, are the gift of Aristodicus.
3. Anonymous epigrammatists
Cypris addressed Eros as he hung his head:
"What grief, my child, has come upon you?" And he answered:
"The Pierians have plundered my apples, one this way, one that,
snatching them from my lap—those I was bringing from Helicon.
Clio took a fifth part of the apples; a twelfth
Euterpe; bright Thalia got an eighth;
Melpomene carried off a twentieth; Terpsichore
a fourth; and Erato came after for a seventh part;
Polymnia robbed me of thirty apples,
and Urania of a hundred and twenty; and Calliope
has gone off weighed down with three hundred apples.
So I come to you with lighter hands,
bringing these fifty apples, what the goddesses have left."
4. Anonymous epigrammatists
On the dung of Augeas
The mighty strength of Alcides asked Augeas,
inquiring after the multitude of his herds; and he answered:
"By the streams of Alpheus, friend, are half of them;
an eighth part graze about the hill of Cronus;
a twelfth, far off, beside the shrine of Taraxippus;
a twentieth feed about divine Elis;
a thirtieth I have left behind in Arcadia;
and the rest of the herds, these fifty, you see here."
5. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am the dark child of a white father, a wingless bird,
flying up even to the clouds of heaven;
and to the maidens who meet me I give birth to tears without grief;
yet, born straightway, I am dissolved into the air.
6. Anonymous epigrammatists
Best of the keepers of the hours, how much of the day has passed?
As much as twice two-thirds of what is gone is what remains.
7. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am a lion of bronze; and my fountains are my two eyes,
and my mouth, and the sole of my right foot.
My right eye fills the bowl in two days,
my left in three, and the sole of my foot in four;
six hours suffice to fill the mouth. With all at once,
mouth and eyes and foot together, say in what time.
8. Anonymous epigrammatists
Six, one, five, two, three, four—so the die runs on.
9. Anonymous epigrammatists
My father-in-law killed my husband, and my husband killed my father-in-law,
and my brother-in-law his father-in-law, and my father-in-law his own father.
10. Anonymous epigrammatists
I have learned that cauldrons are not ones to keep silent,
but rather urge the bronze to ring out true,
the first striking back its echo to the second,
and the third passing it on to the fourth.
But if the mover stays at rest and does not blow,
the cauldron is voiceless; for by nature it is no chatterer.
The nature of your cauldrons, indeed, is fair of mouth;
yet meeting yours it grows fairer still of mouth,
silent when it must be, and speaking when it should.
11. Anonymous epigrammatists
The thousand staters that I have gained
I bid my two sons take;
but let the legitimate one's fifth be increased
by ten of the fourth measure that falls to the bastard.
12. Anonymous epigrammatists
King Croesus dedicated six bowls of six minae,
each one larger than the next by a drachma.
13. Anonymous epigrammatists
Together we two weigh twenty minae,
Zethus and his kinsman; but if you take from me
a third, and the fourth part of this Amphion here,
finding the whole to be six, you will find our mother's weight.
14. Anonymous epigrammatists
One wind; two ships; ten sailors row;
and one helmsman steers them both.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
15. Anonymous epigrammatists
Six feet, in six places, measure out the iambic line:
spondee, choree, dactyl, and anapaest,
pyrrhic and iamb; and each has its own house.
The pyrrhic's end is one that knows a long at the start;
the first and the third and the fifth hold these.
The others march alike along the whole path;
only the lordly iamb the place receives, wherever it will.
16. Anonymous epigrammatists
A whole island, the lowing of an ox, and the voice of a money-lender.
17. Anonymous epigrammatists
The hunt is a rehearsal for war; the hunt teaches
to seize the hidden, to await the attacker, to flee, to pursue.
18. Anonymous epigrammatists
Hector—the man Diomedes slew, that other Hector,
Ajax, who fought before the Trojans with his spear.
19. Anonymous epigrammatists
I once saw a beast running upright on its back
through a wood cut by iron, its feet not touching the ground.
20. Anonymous epigrammatists
If you set in the midst of blazing fire its hundred,
you will find the son and the slayer of a maiden.
21. Anonymous epigrammatists
Casting into the midst of Hephaestus a single hundred,
you will find the son and the slayer of a maiden.
22. Anonymous epigrammatists
Do not speak, and you will speak my name. But must you speak it?
Then thus again—a great marvel—speaking, you will speak my name.
23. Anonymous epigrammatists
Child of Nereus though I am, the son of Earth bears me up,
as I sink down into the lovely streams of Styx.
24. Anonymous epigrammatists
. . . you see me, Dionysus; a twofold womb
bore me, and my father is the lord of memory.
First it bore me a beast-bearer, pitiless of heart;
but when I had slain the dear son of a roe, my own sister's,
no longer do I bear the beast, but heaven and sea,
and earth, and the holy chorus of the blessed, deathless forever.
25. Anonymous epigrammatists
I long for the eyes of Scylla, which the sun himself put out,
and the moon; and my father feared me, his daughter.
I bathe, though dead, in two ever-flowing rivers
that the summit pours forth upon a beetling hill.
26. Anonymous epigrammatists
Once I was a yellow thing, but, when struck,
I become whiter than gleaming snow;
and I delight in the sweet and fish-filled bath,
going first of all the banqueters into the dance.
27. Anonymous epigrammatists
Seeking on the sea the maiden that was once a lion,
you will find the grandmother of child-slaying Hecuba.
28. Anonymous epigrammatists
From the sea I drew a fish-laden race; and a single contest
knows how to lead me to the Dionysiac games;
and, having anointed my body in the stadium with oil,
with my own hands I destroyed the son of Deo;
and again, in the second place, I send forth the Giants,
gathered from here and there, dragged off by many hands.
29. Anonymous epigrammatists
It is given to me alone to join with women in love,
when their own husbands beg it.
30. Anonymous epigrammatists
I have a ram for father, and a tortoise bore me to him;
and at my birth I slew both my parents.
31. Anonymous epigrammatists
Write the second mother of wine, and set upon the limb
a limb; the wife of his fatherland's father you behold.
32. Anonymous epigrammatists
Being slain, I slew my slayer; yet not even so
did he come to Hades; but I, for my part, died.
33. Anonymous epigrammatists
Him who slew me I slew, but I have no joy of it;
for death has made the slain man deathless.
34. Anonymous epigrammatists
There is a city, an island, that drew its blood from a plant's name,
bearing at once an isthmus and a strait upon the mainland;

title: Greek Anthology
text:
there is my blood, and the blood of Cecrops together;
there Hephaestus, rejoicing, holds grey-eyed Athena;
there I bade them send sacrifice to Heracles.
35. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am a limb of man, which even iron cuts;
when a letter is taken away, the sun goes down.
36. Anonymous epigrammatists
Bitter to me is life, sweet is death—and both are water;
I die, pierced by bloodless spears;
and if any, while I yet live, hide me, a corpse, in a tomb,
I am first soaked with the blood of my kindred.
37. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am dear to Pallas, and I bring forth countless children,
which men hurl down from the rocks; and as they perish,
they were a light to Peleus' son, a cure for mortals, a bulwark in contests.
38. Anonymous epigrammatists
I slew my brother, and my brother in turn slew me; we died by our father;
and, both being dead, we slew our mother.
39. Anonymous epigrammatists
Whoever calls me an island will not lie; for in very truth
he has set my name into many roaring noises.
40. Anonymous epigrammatists
There are two sisters, born of the same blood; the one bears
the other, and she who bore is herself born of the other;
so that, being sisters and of the same blood,
they are both, in common, each other's mothers.
41. Anonymous epigrammatists
I give birth to my mother and am born of her; and I am of her
at one time greater, at another smaller.
42. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am a maiden woman, and I am the maiden of a woman,
and year by year, a maiden, I give birth, a woman.
43. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am the image of the sky; two beasts drive me,
one in front, Erigone's, and behind, Pasiphae's;
the bedfellow of Heracles watches over me, and the dear bride
of Phoebus wears me down, often set ablaze.
44. Anonymous epigrammatists
In a single night I came against the Trojans, and the tribes
of the Pelasgians I cut through and took without a spear;
neither the son of Tydeus, nor city-sacking Odysseus,
had strength to drive me, the bold one, out from the ships;
but, swelling with might and courage in my breast,
I destroyed the army of the Argives and of the Phrygians.
45. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am black, white, yellow, dry and moist;
and when you stretch me out above the wooden plains,
I speak to Ares and the hand, though I have no speech.
46. Anonymous epigrammatists
When a letter takes a blow, the name of a foot it makes,
my own; yet it will never let men's feet stumble.
47. Anonymous epigrammatists
For a man's sake I lost my light; and a man, standing by,
gave me a light I love, granting it as a favour to my feet.
48. Anonymous epigrammatists
The Graces were carrying baskets of apples, and in each
was an equal number. The Muses met them,
nine of them, and asked them for apples; and they gave
an equal number to each, and they had—nine and three alike.
Say how many they gave, that all might have equal shares.
49. Anonymous epigrammatists
Make me a crown, mixing gold and bronze,
and tin together with them, and much-wrought iron,
of sixty minae; and let the gold, with the bronze,
be two parts of three; the gold, with the tin together,
three parts of four; and the gold, with the iron,
so many parts of five. Tell me, then, how much you must mix
of gold, and how much of bronze; and tell me still
how much of tin, and say how much of the remaining iron,
that you may make for me the crown of sixty minae.
50. Anonymous epigrammatists
Add a third, silversmith, and the fourth
of the bowl into one, and the twelfth as well;
then drive it into the furnace, and, when all is stirred,

title: Greek Anthology
text:
draw me out the lump, and let it weigh a mina for me.
51. Anonymous epigrammatists
A. I have the next man's share, and a third of the third's.
B. And I the next man's share, and a third of the first's.
C. And I ten minae, and a third of the middle one's.
52. Anonymous epigrammatists
On wine
There was a time when, with the Lapiths and valiant Heracles,
I destroyed in battle the two-formed Centaurs;
there was a time when the only-begotten maiden died of three blows
of mine, and I grieved the son of Cronus who dwells in the sea;
but now the third Muse beholds me, mingled with the fiery Nymphs,
lying upon a floor of glass.
53. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a lamp
Pallas once, overcome in the arms of Hephaestus,
went to his bed in the chamber of Peleus;
and when they had covered themselves in shining linen,
at once was born the night-faring Phaethon.
54. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a cupping-glass
The cunning craft of Paeon made me too breathe in fire,
hidden beneath lips of beaten bronze;
and, drawing the dark blood from feeble men,
I slay Hephaestus, holding him close within my belly.
55. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a clyster
To me alone among women it is right to join
openly in love, when husbands beg it;
and I alone go in to youths, and men, and old men,
and to maidens, to the grief of their parents.
I hate lewdness; but the healer's hand loves me,
while I accomplish the labour of Amphitryon's son.
For those who are tended I would fight even with Pluto,
ever for the life of all whom I have joined with.
A keen-scented child with white teeth I am made
by men's skill—ivory mingled with the goat.
56. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a mirror
If you look at me, I too look at you. You look with your eyelids,
but I not with eyelids; for I have no eyelids.
And, if you wish, I speak without a voice; for yours it is
to have a voice, while in me the lips are opened in vain.
57. Anonymous epigrammatists
On the date of the palm
I have my mother's name; I am sweeter than she who bore me;
but she is long, and I am little;
she is not to be eaten, save for her head; but I
am wholly to be eaten, only my inwards are not.
58. Anonymous epigrammatists
On the artichoke
I carry a brain without a head; and I am green,
lifted from the earth on a long neck;
I look like a ball upon a pipe; and, if you search
within my flanks, I have my mother's father.
59. Anonymous epigrammatists
On the Argo
Having received fifty sons in a single womb,
. . . I slew the leader of all the . . .
And he has died twice, since two wombs
bore him—one of bronze, and before it, one of man.
60. Anonymous epigrammatists
A writing-tablet
The wood begot me, and iron made me new;
I am the secret receptacle of the Muses;
shut, I am silent; but I speak when you open me wide,
having Ares alone as the partner of my words.
61. Anonymous epigrammatists
In the mountains I was born; a tree was my mother,
fire my father; and I am a darkening clod;
but if my father melt me within deep clay,
I heal the wounds of the sea-borne ship.
62. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a ball
I am very hairy, but my leaves hide
my hairs, so that no hole appears anywhere;
by many children I am played with; and if any is
clumsy at the throw, he stands like an ass.
63. Mesomedes
Creeping, flying, walking, a maiden,
a running lioness lifting a bastard track,
winged was she, in front a woman,
in the middle a roaring lioness, a beast,
and behind, a coiling serpent.
Neither did her trailing length run off as a serpent, nor as a woman,
nor as a bird in her whole body, nor as a beast;

title: Greek Anthology
text:
for she appeared a maiden without feet,
and the roaring beast had no head.
She had a nature confusedly mixed,
things unfinished and finished blended together.
64. Anonymous epigrammatists
The riddle of the Sphinx
There is on the earth a two-footed thing, and four-footed, with one voice,
and three-footed; alone it changes its form of all the creatures
that move upon the earth, and through the air, and over the sea.
But whenever it walks supported on the most feet,
then is the speed of its limbs at its very feeblest.
65. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Homer
There is an island, Ios, your mother's homeland, which, when you are dead,
will receive you; but beware the riddle of the young boys.
66. Anonymous epigrammatists
Another, to the same man
Blessed and ill-fated—for you were born to both—
you seek your homeland; but it is your mother's, not your father's,
a mother-city in an island, off broad Crete,
the land of Minos, neither near nor far away;
there it is your fated portion to end your life,
when, hearing it from the tongue of boys, you cannot make out
a hymn hard to grasp, spoken in crooked words.
For you have drawn a twofold portion of life: the one dim,
of two suns, the other equal to the immortals' share,
in life and in death; and dead you shall yet be far from age.
67. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Laius the Theban
Laius, son of Labdacus, you ask for a blessed race of children.
I will give you a dear son; but it is fated
that you will leave the light by your own son's hands; for so I have nodded assent.
68. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Carystus
Dear child of glorious Chiron, Carystus,
leaving Pelion, come to the headland of Euboea;
there it is decreed for you to found a holy land.
69. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Lycurgus
You come, Lycurgus, to my rich temple,
dear to Zeus and to all who hold the Olympian halls.
I am in doubt whether to prophesy you a god or a man;
but rather, even more, I hope you are a god, Lycurgus.
70. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given from Sarapis
Do not blame your fate, nor the gods at all, stranger;
blame rather the hour in which your father sowed you.
71. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle of the Pythia
Pure, stranger, come to the precinct of the pure god,
having touched the nymph's running water in your soul;
for to the good a small drop suffices; but a base man
not even all Ocean could wash clean with its streams.
72. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Rufinus, who asked how he might take an oath from his own ship's captain
When the Titan lifts his early course above the earth,
loosing with his rays the harms of murky night,
and Dawn, the early-born, shines forth her radiant new light,
then, leading the man down beside the shores and the sea-sprayed beaches,
set him facing toward the light of the sun's beam.
Let him hold his right foot within the stream,
set in the eddies, and let him plant his left foot firm upon the ground;
and, touching with his hands on either side,
with one the sea and with the other the dry land, to confirm the oath
let him swear by heaven, and the boundless earth, and the harbours of the sea,
and the life-giving lord of the heavenly fire;
for such an oath the gods themselves do not dare
to slight upon their lips, the proud sons of Heaven.
73. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to the Megarians
Of all the land, Pelasgian Argos is best,
the mares of Thessaly, and the women of Lacedaemon,
and the men who drink the water of fair Arethusa;

title: Greek Anthology
text:
but better still than these are they who dwell between
Tiryns and sheep-rich Arcadia,
the linen-corseleted Argives, the goads of war;
but you, Megarians, are not third, nor fourth,
nor twelfth—not to be reckoned in word or in number.
74. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle of the Pythia
The shrines of the gods stand open to the good, nor is there need
of purifications; no pollution touches virtue.
But whoever is baneful of heart, depart; for never
will a drenched body wash your soul clean.
75. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given in Heliopolis, when the columns of the temple of Zeus that was there suffered shipwreck—the columns that are now in Berytus
Say to Poseidon: "It is fitting to obey
elder brothers; you take no proper pride
in the columns of my glorious court." Say it, having shaken
three times the gleaming sea, and he will obey. But if he disobeys,
let him take heed, lest I set the whole sea ablaze;
for not even the sea quenches the thunderbolt of Zeus.
76. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle of the Pythia
You ask me for Arcadia; you ask a great thing; I will not give it you;
many acorn-eating men are in Arcadia,
who will hinder you; yet I begrudge you nothing.
I will give you Tegea to dance with stamping feet,
and a fair plain to measure out with the line.
77. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle reported in the Lives of Theseus
Blessed is this man, who now over the stone threshold
mounts up to the oracle of Phoebus Apollo,
come in search of good government; and I, for my part,
will give you what no other city upon earth shall have.
78. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle of the Pythia
There is a Tegea of Arcadia, in a level place;
there two winds blow under strong constraint,
and stroke lies against counter-stroke, and woe upon woe;
there the life-giving earth holds the son of Agamemnon's son;
bring him home, and you will be the protector of Tegea.
79. Anonymous epigrammatists
Of Lydian race, king of many, great fool Croesus,
do not wish to hear within your halls the long-prayed-for voice
of your son speaking; far better for you that it be
otherwise; for he will first speak on a day of misfortune.
80. Anonymous epigrammatists
The fated portion it is impossible
to escape, even for a god.
81. Anonymous epigrammatists
Do not burn through the isthmus, nor dig it;
for Zeus would have made it an island, had he wished.
82. Anonymous epigrammatists
But when in Siphnos the town-halls turn white,
and the marketplace is white-browed, then indeed there is need of a man of sense
to beware a wooden ambush and a red herald.
83. Anonymous epigrammatists
Battus, you have come for a voice; but lord Phoebus Apollo
sends you to sheep-rearing Libya as its founder.
84. Anonymous epigrammatists
If you know sheep-rearing Libya better than I,
without having gone there, while I have gone—much do I admire your wisdom.
85. Anonymous epigrammatists
Whoever shall come later to lovely Libya,
when the land is being parcelled out, I say he shall one day be sorry for it.
86. Anonymous epigrammatists
Eetion, no one honours you, though you are full worthy of honour.
Labda is with child, and shall bear a rolling stone; it shall fall
upon men who are monarchs, and shall set Corinth to rights.
87. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle
An eagle is with young among the rocks, and shall bear a lion,
mighty, raw-devouring; and he shall loose the knees of many.
88. Anonymous epigrammatists
Blessed is this man, who comes down into my house,
Cypselus, son of Eetion, king of famous Corinth,

title: Greek Anthology
text:
himself and his sons—but no longer his sons' sons.
89. Anonymous epigrammatists
And then indeed, Miletus, contriver of evil deeds,
you shall become a feast and splendid spoils for many;
and your wives shall wash the feet of many long-haired men;
and the care of my temple at Didyma shall fall to others.
90. Anonymous epigrammatists
But when the female, having vanquished the male,
drives him out, and wins glory among the Argives,
then she shall make many Argive women tear their cheeks;
so that one day a man among those yet to come will say:
"A dread serpent, uncoiled, perished, subdued by the spear."
91. Anonymous epigrammatists
Glaucus, son of Epicydes, for the moment this is more profitable—
to win by an oath and plunder the goods.
Swear, then; for death awaits even the man true to his oath.
But Oath has a son, nameless, with no hands
and no feet; yet swiftly he comes on, until he seizes
and destroys the whole race and the whole house.
But the race of the man true to his oath is better hereafter.
92. Anonymous epigrammatists
Wretched ones, why do you sit? Leave and flee to the ends of the earth,
your homes, and the topmost heights of your wheel-shaped city.
For neither the head shall stay firm, nor the body,
nor the lowest feet, nor the hands, nor anything of the middle
is left, but all is wretched; for fire lays it low,
and keen Ares, driving on the Syrian chariot;
and many other towers besides he shall destroy, not yours alone,
and many temples of the immortals he shall give to ravening fire,
which now, I think, stand streaming with sweat,
quaking with fear; and down the topmost roofs
dark blood is poured, foreseeing the doom of disaster.
But go forth from the shrine, and pour out your spirit upon your woes.
93. Anonymous epigrammatists
Pallas cannot appease Olympian Zeus,
though she entreat him with many words and shrewd counsel;
but to you I will speak this word again, making it hard as adamant.
When all the rest is taken, all that the bound of Cecrops
holds within, and the hollow of holy Cithaeron,
far-thundering Zeus grants to Tritogeneia a wall of wood
alone to remain unsacked, which shall profit you and your children.
And do not stay at rest to await the horse and the foot,
the great army coming from the mainland, but withdraw,
turning your back; yet one day you shall stand against them.
O divine Salamis, you shall destroy the children of women,
whether Demeter is scattered or gathered in.
94. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle of the Pythia
Hateful to your neighbours, dear to the immortal gods,
sit guarded, holding your spear within,
and guard your head; and it will save the body too.
95. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle
Foolish men, you blame as coming from Menelaus' vengeance
the tears that Minos, in his wrath, has sent you—
because they did not help him to avenge the death
that came to him in Camicus, while you for them
avenged the woman snatched from Sparta by a barbarian man.
96. Anonymous epigrammatists
To you, dwellers in spacious Sparta,
either the great and glorious city is sacked by the men
of Perseus' line; or, if not that, the bound of Lacedaemon
shall mourn a king dead, of the stock of Heracles.
For neither the might of bulls nor of lions
shall hold him back face to face; for he has the might of Zeus; nor do I say
he shall be held, until he has torn one of these two utterly apart.
97. Athenaeus
An oracle of the Pythia
Take heed, when the barbarian-tongued one casts a yoke of papyrus
upon the sea, to keep the loud-bleating goats away from Euboea.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
98. Athenaeus
An oracle of Bacis concerning the victory of the Greeks
But when they bridge with ships the holy shore
of golden-sworded Artemis and sea-girt Cynosura,
in maddened hope, having sacked shining Athens,
divine Justice shall quench mighty Insolence, son of Outrage,
raging dreadful, thinking to overcome all things.
For bronze shall mingle with bronze, and Ares with blood
shall redden the sea; then the day of freedom for Greece
far-thundering Zeus brings on, and lady Victory.
99. Athenaeus
The gathering of the Greeks by Thermodon and grassy Asopus,
and the barbarian-tongued battle-cry,
where many shall fall beyond their lot and their doom,
of the bow-bearing Medes, when the appointed day comes.
100. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Menelaus and Alexander
Why have you two kings, the one of the Trojans, the other of the Achaeans,
not of one mind, come up into my house—
the one, indeed, seeking to find the offspring of a mare,
the other to lead the mare away? What now will you devise, great Zeus?
101. Cleobulus
One is the father, and the children twelve; and of each
are children twice thirty, of twofold appearance:
some of them are white to look upon, and others black;
and, though immortal, they all perish.
102. Anonymous epigrammatists
From the Pythia, to the emperor Hadrian
You ask of me, the unknown, the race and homeland
of the ambrosial Siren; some Ithaca of Homer is my seat;
Telemachus was my father, and Nestor's Polycaste
my mother, who bore him wiser than all other mortals.
103. Anonymous epigrammatists
On a raisin
If you had taken me young, you might soon have drunk my spilled blood;
but now, when time has made me old,
eat me, wrinkled, having nothing moist,
crushing my bones together with my flesh.
104. Anonymous epigrammatists
A pouch on your back, a basket in your hand, a he-goat on your shoulders—
goatherd, you carry all the tokens of your fields.
105. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am a lowly limb of living things; but if you take from me
a single letter, I become another part of the head;
if another, I shall be a living creature again; and if yet another,
you will find not one, but two hundred.
106. Anonymous epigrammatists
With four letters I make my way along the path; but if you take
the first letter away, I hear; and the next after that again—
you will find me dearest to the mire; and if you lift the last,
you will find an adverb of place.
107. Anonymous epigrammatists
Eros has hurled forth his torch and his bow and his arrows,
and pours out, instead of darts, the dust of the Ethiopians.
108. Anonymous epigrammatists
I have nothing within, and yet all is within me,
and freely, for my virtue, I give grace to all.
109. Anonymous epigrammatists
A maiden, laid in the fire, died; and the betrayer
was wine; and that by which she died was a shoot of Pallas;
her slayer was a shipwrecked man; and in a living tomb
she lies, blaming the favours of Bromius.
109a. Anonymous epigrammatists
Pallas and Bromius and the famous Lame One,
these three made away with the one and only maiden.
110. Anonymous epigrammatists
No one seeing sees me, but the unseeing beholds;
he who speaks not speaks, he who runs not runs;
and I am false, though I tell all truths.
111. Anonymous epigrammatists
Childless of childless ones, dart-bearing, the babe within, the lifting up.
112. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Croesus the Lydian
But when a mule becomes king over the Medes,
then indeed, tender-footed Lydian, by the pebble-strewn Hermus

title: Greek Anthology
text:
flee, and do not stay, nor be ashamed to be a coward.
113. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Archilochus
Deathless and renowned in song, Telesicles, shall your son be
among men—he who shall be the first to greet you
as you step from your ship in your dear native land.
114. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to the mother of Alexander in Cyzicus
The Persians slew my servant, my commander, with violent hand,
and his own dust covers his corpse;
and if any should swiftly show his white bones to Phaethon,
that man shall shatter the great power of the Persians from within;
he lies within an island bounded by the coast of Asia,
beside laurel and streams, by aged Pelion;
and mark a man, a seer, a guide of the road,
a Phocian, who dwells in the sands of Aparnis.
115. Anonymous epigrammatists
Constantine, having come near to Troy, wished to found there a royal city; and receiving the oracle, he departed and founded Constantinople.
It is not lawful for you, on a foundation cut down long ago at Troy,
to set up the new name of Rome; go rejoicing
to the Megarian town beside the sea of the Propontis,
where fish and deer feed on the same pasture.
116. Anonymous epigrammatists
Why do you press me with blows for the sake of the nuts,
mother? Fair maidens shared all these out among them.
For Melission took two-sevenths of mine,
and Titane took a twelfth; a sixth and a third
are held by Astyoche and Philinna, fond of play;
Thetis snatched and took twenty, Thisbe twelve;
and look—Glauce laughs sweetly, holding in her hands
eleven; and this one nut alone is left to me.
117. Anonymous epigrammatists
A. Where have your apples gone, my child? B. Ino has two-sixths,
and Semele holds an eighth part;
Autonoe carried off a fourth; and Agave
went off snatching a fifth from my lap;
ten apples are kept for yourself; but I—
yes, by dear Cypris—have this one only.
118. Anonymous epigrammatists
Myrto, having once plucked apples, shared them among her friends:
to Chrysis she gave a fifth of the apples, to Hero a fourth,
a nineteenth to Psamathe, a tenth to Cleopatra;
and a twentieth she gave to Parthenopeia;
but to Euadne she gave twelve alone; and to herself
came, out of all, a hundred and twenty apples.
119. Anonymous epigrammatists
Once, meeting their friends, Ino and Semele shared out apples
among twelve maidens.
And to some Semele gave even numbers; to others odd
her sister gave; and she had the more apples.
For Semele gave three-sevenths to three companions,
and to two she gave a fifth of all as their share;
eleven Astynome took from her, and there were left her
only two apples to bear to her sisters.
But the other gave to four maidens two-fourths of her apples,
and to a fifth she gave a sixth part to keep;
four she gave as a gift to Eurychore; and with four other
apples Semele remained, rejoicing.
120. Anonymous epigrammatists
The nut-tree was laden with many nuts;
but now someone of a sudden has stripped it bare. But what does it say?
"Of my nuts Parthenopeia took a fifth;
an eighth share Philinna carries off; and Aganippe
a fourth; in a seventh Oreithyia delights;
a sixth share of nuts Eurynome plucked;
three times six and a hundred the Graces shared among them;
and nine times nine the Muses took of mine; and the remaining seven
you will find sitting on the topmost boughs."
121. Anonymous epigrammatists
From Gadira to the seven-hilled city: a sixth of the road
as far as the loud-lowing shores of Baetis;
thence again a fifth to the Phocian land of Pylades,

title: Greek Anthology
text:
the Taurian country, named from its fine cattle;
from there, as you go on to steep-horned Pyrene,
an eighth, and a twelfth of a single tenth.
Between Pyrene and the high-headed Alps
a fourth; and straightway a twelfth of Ausonia,
where it begins, the amber of Eridanus shines forth.
O blessed I, who have accomplished two thousand stades,
and, driving on still five hundred more from there—
for the Tarpeian palace was my care.
122. Anonymous epigrammatists
Having defiled the holy veils of fair-eyed Justice,
that I might gaze on you, all-subduing gold, for so long,
I have nothing; for four tens of talents I gave in vain
to friends of ill omen for no good;
and a half, and a third, and an eighth, O manifold
dooms of men, I see in the hands of an enemy.
123. Anonymous epigrammatists
Take a fifth of the inheritance, my son; and a twelfth
receive, my wife; and you, four children of my departed son,
and two brothers, and my much-groaning mother,
let each have an eleventh part of the estate.
But you, my nephews, receive twelve talents;
and let Eubulus, my friend, have five talents.
To my most faithful slaves, freedom and a reward,
the wage of their service—this I give to these:
let them take it thus: let Onesimus have twenty-five
minae; let Daos have twenty minae,
Syrus fifty, Synete ten, Tibius eight;
and seven minae I give to Synete, the child of Syrus.
From thirty talents adorn my tomb,
and perform a sacrifice to Zeus of the Underworld
for the two—both for the pyre and the barley-meal and the fillets;
let the body of the two receive its due thanks.
124. Anonymous epigrammatists
The sun, the moon, and the wandering stars that run round
the zodiac, spun for you such a destiny:
a sixth part of your life to remain, an orphan,
beside your dear mother; an eighth in hardship,
to serve among your enemies; and after that, on the third portion,
the gods will grant you a return home, a wife, and a beloved child;
then indeed your child and your wife shall perish
under Scythian spears. And you, having poured out tears for those sorrows,
at seven and twenty years shall pass to the end of your life.
125. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am a tomb; and I hold the much-bewailed children of Philinna,
such fruit of her ill-childbearing womb:
a fifth among the youths, a third among the maidens,
and three newly wedded girls Philinna gave me;
and the rest, four from her womb, bereft utterly of sun
and of voice, fell into Acheron.
126. Anonymous epigrammatists
This tomb holds Diophantus—ah, great marvel—
and the tomb tells, by its art, the measure of his life.
A sixth part of his life the god granted him to be a boy;
adding a twelfth, he clothed his cheeks with down;
and after a seventh part he kindled for him the light of marriage,
and five years after the marriage he granted him a child.
Alas, the late-born, wretched child—half his father's
span the cold grave took, after taking the measure of his life.
And for four years more, consoling his grief,
by the science of numbers he came to the end of his life.
127. Anonymous epigrammatists
Of all the time he lived, a fourth Demochares
lived as a boy; a fifth as a youth;
a third entering manhood; and when grey old age came on,
he lived the remaining thirteen years on the threshold of age.
128. Anonymous epigrammatists
How my brother has done me violence, dividing the five talents
of our father's goods in no holy portion.
Seven of these elevenths of my brother's share, in many tears,
I have, but a fifth of the portion. Zeus, you are in a deep sleep.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
129. Anonymous epigrammatists
Someone said to the helmsman, as he cut the broad passage of the Adriatic
with his ship: "How many measures of the sea are yet left?"
And he answered him: "Sailor, from the brow of Cretan Crios
to Sicilian Pelorias are six times
a thousand measures; and of the course already past,
twice two-fifths is left to the Sicilian strait."
130. Anonymous epigrammatists
Of the four spouts, one filled the whole
cistern in a day, this one in two, this in three days,
and the fourth in four. In what time will they all fill it?
131. Anonymous epigrammatists
Open me, and in four hours I will fill the cistern
that stands here, a spout pouring forth abundantly;
my right-hand fellow falls short of me by as many hours
before it fills it; and the third by twice as many.
But if you bid both pour out their stream of water with me,
in a small part of a day we shall fill it.
132. Anonymous epigrammatists
I am the Cyclops Polyphemus, made of bronze; and on me
someone has wrought an eye and a mouth and a hand,
joining them to spouts; and I seem to be wholly dripping,
and still I am seen gushing from my mouth.
But none of the spouts is irregular: the hand, in three days alone,
pouring forth, will fill the cistern;
the eye, in a day; and the mouth in two-fifths of a day.
Who could tell what time the three running together would take?
133. Anonymous epigrammatists
How good it is that these two swift rivers
mingle their stream into the bowl, with the Grace of Bromius.
But the course of the streams is not equal for all; rather Nile alone,
pouring on, will fill it in a day,
so much water does he belch from his breasts; and from Bacchus
the thyrsus, in three days, sends forth its wine;
and your horn, Achelous, in two days. Now all together
flow, and you will fill it in a few hours.
134. Anonymous epigrammatists
O woman, how you have forgotten your poverty—poverty that lies
ever upon you with the necessary goads of toil.
A mina of wool you used to spin in a day; the elder
of your daughters drew out a mina and a third of the weft;
the younger bore the half of one. But now, with all of them at once,
you make ready supper, having drawn out but a single mina.
135. Anonymous epigrammatists
We three bath-pouring Loves stand here,
sending baths upon the fair-flowing channel.
I, the right-hand one, from my long-winged ankles
will fill this in a sixth part of a day;
the left, again, from his jar in four hours;
and the middle one, from his bow, in the very middle of the day.
Consider, then, in how short a time we might fill it,
pouring at once from wings and bow and jar.
136. Anonymous epigrammatists
Brick-makers, I am most eager to raise up this house,
and this day is cloudless today; nor do I need
many more, having all the brick but three hundred short.
You alone made so many in a day;
but your son left off two hundred short of the labour,
and your son-in-law again so many, and yet fifty more.
In how many hours will the three teams build this?
137. Anonymous epigrammatists
Dropping a tear beside us, pass on; for we are those
whom this fallen house of Antiochus destroyed,
his banqueters; and a god granted us a tomb equal
to our feast, and this place for our burial. Four of us
from Tegea lie here; twelve from Messene; and five
from Argos; and from Sparta half the banqueters,
and Antiochus himself; and a fifth of a fifth perished,
the sons of Cecrops; and you, Corinth, weep for Hylas alone.
138. Anonymous epigrammatists
Nicarete, playing with five companions of her own age,

title: Greek Anthology
text:
of the nuts she had gave Clio a third,
and a fourth to Sappho, and a fifth to Aristodice,
a twentieth to Theano, and again a twelfth,
and a twenty-fourth to Philinnis; and there were left over
to Nicarete herself fifty nuts.
139. Anonymous epigrammatists
Diodorus, great glory of the sundial-makers, tell me the hour
at which from the east the golden wheels of the sun
leapt up to the pole. "Of his course as much as three-fifths
is now gone, and four times as much again is left until the western sea."
140. Anonymous epigrammatists
Blessed Zeus, were these deeds truly pleasing to you, such as the women
of Thessaly play at? The eye of Selene fades
before mortal men; I saw it myself; and there was still until dawn
of the departing night twice as much as two-sixths and a seventh.
141. Anonymous epigrammatists
Of the fixed stars, and the passings of the wanderers besides,
tell me, when yesterday my wife was in labour.
"The day was as much as twice a seventh from the rising,
and six times as much it was until the western sea."
142. Anonymous epigrammatists
Awake! Dawn has run past us; a fifth of the day, workers,
is gone, leaving three of the eighths behind.
143. Anonymous epigrammatists
In the shoals of the Syrtis my father died. And from that voyage
this one, the foremost of my brothers, came home
bringing five talents; for to me indeed
he gave twice two-thirds of his portion,
and to my mother two-eighths of our share
he granted, nor did he miss the justice of the immortals.
144. Anonymous epigrammatists
A. The base on which I tread, with me, draws what a weight!
B. And the pedestal, with me, bears so many talents.
A. But I, alone, draw up your base twice over;
B. And I, being alone, lift your base three times.
145. Anonymous epigrammatists
A. Give me ten minae, and I become three times yours.
B. And I, taking the same from you, am five times yours.
146. Anonymous epigrammatists
A. Give me two minae, and I become double yours.
B. And I, taking the same from you, am four times yours.
147. Homerus
Homer, to Hesiod, who asked how great was the number of the Greeks
that marched against Ilium
Seven were the hearths of ravening fire; and on each
were fifty spits, and around them fifty pieces of meat;
and three times three hundred Achaeans there were about each single piece.
148. Germanus
An oracle given to Julian the Apostate, when, keeping his birthday, he was passing the time near Ctesiphon, watching the chariot-races
Once the counsellor Zeus slew the race of the Earth-born,
most hateful to the blessed ones who hold the Olympian halls.
The godlike king of the Romans, Julian,
warring against cities upon cities and long walls
of close-fighting men, laid them waste with fire and mighty iron,
and unceasingly subdued many nations besides;
he too, taking by close-pressed battles the Alamannic soil
of the men of the West, ravaged their fields.
149. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Timocrates the Athenian, who asked concerning epilepsy
Lifting from the head of a fleecy bleating sheep
a worm grown large, lay it about the body of the field-roaming flock,
a wide-wandering creeper from the head of the well-fleeced beast.
150. Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Aegeus, who asked concerning the begetting of children
The jutting foot of the wineskin, dearest of men,
do not loose, until you come to the height of Athens.
1. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the little poem of John the Grammarian
The image-maker dared to paint what no portrait may lawfully show,
and eloquence brought to completion a deceptive likeness of the world,
near to the truth — yet the painting falsified everything.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
2. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the city of Myra in Lycia
This wall of the city of fair dancing-grounds was raised on high
by the sceptred Marcian, at the prompting of the prefect
Palladius, and by the ordinances of prudent Artemeon;
and the city in time recovered its former measure.
3. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the tomb of Saint Nicander
Seventeen years old, a child unstained and undefiled,
God made me, Nicander, his faithful martyr.
4. Anonymous Epigrammatists
A funeral inscription at Nicaea, near the lake, upon the obelisk
Boast, Nicaea, of this tomb that storms the heavens,
and of this pyramid, neighbour to the sun;
it hides the hierophant, famed among the living,
buried within this immeasurable monument.
This is the great barrow of Sacerdos, this the memorial
of Severa, whose neighbour is heaven, not Hades.
5. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Heavenly is the monument and the gold-wrought beam of light
of the man who found a tomb the equal of his life,
neighbour to the stars; it bears such a man as no tomb ever held,
the minister of the heavenly mystery,
who lifted up his fallen homeland from the ground,
who won the highest honours of mind and of speech;
for whom Attica strove, she who set his corpse upon the fire,
and she who received his bones into her bosom.
6. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This great monument of great Sacerdos was wrought,
all-radiant, an earthly star of Ascania,
facing the sunbeams; and within, the spirit lies at peace,
he who stretched out his right hand even to his homeland
as it lay prostrate, and bound about his brows the holy garland,
renewed for the son from the father;
his homeland received him, a beloved corpse, Attica hallowed him
on the pyre, and all the cities of Hellas revere him.
7. Anonymous Epigrammatists
My homeland is Nicaea, my father the revealer of heaven's
mysteries, and I am the heir of the rite;
he it was who rescued my city, when it was shaken, from Hades
by the gifts of Italian Zeus;
I die far from Ascania, and upon the land
of ancient Attica I mounted the pyre.
A conspicuous monument was won for me by my son,
namesake of his grandfather; and his virtue looks to us both.
8. Anonymous Epigrammatists
One marriage was ours, a common life, nor even in death
have we two ceased to remember each other;
and you, Sacerdos, the mysteries and the works of a man
shall proclaim your life to all the days to come;
but me, Severa, my husband, my child, my character, my beauty
shall make more sung than Penelope of old.
9. Flavius Cyrus
An encomium on Theodosius the emperor
You bear all the renowned works of the son of Aeacus,
save the love that ambushed him; you shoot your arrows like Teucer,
yet you keep no bastard's lot, and you have a glorious form,
the form of Agamemnon, but wine does not stir your wits;
in prudence I liken you wholly to keen-witted Odysseus,
yet far from the wicked guiles; and of the old man of Pylos
you distil an equal honey-sweet voice, my king,
before in time you reach and touch the third generation.
10. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Whence found we witnesses upon the deep? Tell us, you rocks,
tell us, you long waves, with how many storms they battled.
The ship was broken, the mast fell, the keel sank, the cargo was lost.
11. Anonymous Epigrammatists
In the citadel of Lindus
Wide is the fame of ancient Lindus, who upon her heights
that touch the sky received the Unwearied Maiden;
but greater still upon the earth grew the lovely renown
of the virgin, when she was filled with grey-eyed graces.
For now the place cries aloud that it is the flourishing house
of Athena, looking out upon the fruit-bearing crags;
this sweet offering the priest Aglochartus gave to Athena,
sharing it from his own possessions,
stronger than the lands of Celeus and of Icarius
wholly to increase the holy olive.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
12. Leo the Philosopher
Well do you treat me, Fortune, tending me with the most pleasant
freedom from troubles of Epicurus, and delighting me with quiet;
why then should I have need of men's care-laden busyness?
I do not want wealth, that blind and fickle friend,
nor honours; for the honours of mortals are a feeble dream.
Away from me, dark cave of Circe; for I am ashamed,
born for heaven, to eat acorns like a beast;
I hate the sweet food of the Lotus-eaters, that makes a man forget his country;
the alluring song of the Sirens I reject as my enemy;
but I pray to receive from God the soul-saving flower,
the moly, the defence against evil opinions, and stopping my ears
securely with wax, to flee the desire bred in my flesh.
Saying and writing these things, may I reach the end of my life.
13. Constantine
On his own throne
If you are wise, sit down; but if of the Muse
with your fingertip you have only barely tasted, . . .
stand far from me, and seek your seat elsewhere;
for I am a chair that carries men who know wisdom.
14. Theophanes the Confessor
A reply to this
And what special mark do you bear, O vainglorious one,
that you love the wise and drive away the unlettered?
You wear no gold, no silver, no ivory,
but the men who are masters of carpentry made you,
ignorant of Calliope and untaught of Hephaestus,
to be a wooden seat for the wise and the unwise alike.
15. Constantine
On the cross which he dedicated in Lindus
Constantine, son of John and Eudocia,
made me, his glorious offering, whom proud Lindus
brought forth as a man more excellent than the former generation,
a faithful servant of the sceptred Leo;
with whom his brother Alexander and his son Constantine
together led the god-supported sceptres of the empire.
16. Constantine
On the same cross
Every work falls short of your worth,
O Mistress of the world, beyond all wonder;
for your glory is beyond all works and beyond decay;
yet this work, which Constantine has offered you,
is worthy, if indeed, O Virgin,
it well portrays the sceptre of your offspring,
and the thrice-blessed Passion of his flesh.
17. Constantine
On the icon of the Mother of God
If anyone wished to paint you, O Virgin,
he would need the stars rather than colours,
that you might be drawn with lights, as the gate of light;
but these things do not yield to the words of mortals;
so what nature has granted and the law of painting,
with these we depict and portray you on our part.
18. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the gaming-board
Your bones, Palamedes, ought to have been sawn
into the instruments of the art that comes from war;
for while you were in wars, you revealed another war,
upon a wooden field, the war of friends.
19. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On a certain physician, Asclepiades
The physician Asclepiades carried off a girl by force.
And after the ruin of the marriage won by abduction
he called a crowd to the lawless wedding,
of dancing men and wretched women;
but the house collapsed in the evening,
and all were brought down to the halls of Hades,
corpses lay fallen upon corpses;
and the stately bridal chamber, woven of roses,
dripped crimson blood from the slaughter.
20. Palladas
In silence pass through this wretched life,
imitating in your silence time itself;
live unnoticed, and if not, then die unnoticed.
21. Theocritus
Bedfellow of no one, and mother of Far-fighting War,
she bore the swift guide of the midwife counter-rock,
not Cerastes, whom once the bull-fathered one reared,
but him whose end once burned away the mind before the shield's rim,
a whole name, of double nature, who held the longing
of the windswept, voice-bearing daughter of Merops;
who fashioned a shrill song for the violet-crowned Muse,
a wound, an ornament of fire-crackling desire;
who quenched the equal-voiced manhood
of the grandfather-slain, and the Tyrian . . . ,
to whom Paris Simichidas set this lovely
possession of the blind-bearing one.
A soul, O cattle-treading,
gadfly of the standing Saettan,
of stolen father, fatherless,
chest-limbed, rejoicing,
may you sing sweetly
to the mute girl,
to Calliope,
unseen.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
22. Simias
To be written thus:
A gift to man-goddess Athena the Phocian gave, repaying the grace of mighty counsel,
at that time when, with fire-breathing wax, he set ablaze the holy city
— not counted among the foremost fighters of the Achaeans,
but now he has gone upon the Homeric road,
thrice blessed, on whom in your heart
this happiness
breathes ever.
Look graciously about us.
For your grace, holy and full-counselling Pallas;
but, in disgrace, bring the stream from the pure springs;
of the sons of Dardanus, and the gold-dyed lords he hurled from their foundations;
Epeius gave the axe, with which once he cast down the height of the god-built towers.
To be read thus:
A gift to man-goddess Athena the Phocian gave, repaying the grace of mighty counsel,
Epeius gave the axe, with which once he cast down the height of the god-built towers,
at that time when, with fire-breathing wax, he set ablaze the holy city
of the sons of Dardanus, and the gold-dyed lords he hurled from their foundations;
— not counted among the foremost fighters of the Achaeans,
but, in disgrace, brought the stream from the pure springs upon the road;
but now he has gone upon the Homeric road,
for your grace, holy and full-counselling Pallas;
thrice blessed, on whom in your heart
you look graciously about us.
This happiness
breathes ever.
23. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the book of Mark
If you wish to master grief,
unfolding this blessed book
go through it carefully,
beneath whose most blessed judgement
readily you will see the things to come,
the things that are and the things gone by,
that delight and pain alike
are nothing better than smoke.
24. Simias
Behold me, lord of deep-bosomed Earth, who set the son of Acmon elsewhere,
and do not tremble, though so great, that I am laden with shaggy thick beard.
For I came to be at the time when Necessity ruled,
and all things yielded to Earth's grievous designs,
the creeping things, all that creep
through the air.
And of Chaos
I am born; not the child of Cypris,
swift-flying, nor am I called of Ares;
for I ruled not by force, but by soft-spoken persuasion;
and Earth yielded to me, and the recesses of the Sea, and the brazen Heaven;
from these I took for myself the primeval sceptre, and I ordained the laws for the gods.
25. Besantinus
The brine of holy things wets me not
with its drops, as the murex
stains with its purple ooze;
and the Naxian knives, whetted upon the stone,
spared the possessions of Pan; not with eddying smoke
does the fragrant birdlime blacken me of the Nysian shoots.
For you see me as an altar made neither of bricks
of gold nor fixed of the lumps of Alybe;
nor that one which the Cynthus-born race fashioned,
taking the horns of the bleating goats,
about the smooth ridges
that the Cynthian goats graze —
none such may be set as equal to me.
For with the offspring of Heaven
the earth-born ninefold company made me;
and the king of the immortals nodded assent
to their ever-living craft.
But you, who have drunk of the fountain
which the son of the Gorgon cleft,
sacrifice and pour libation to me
a draught far sweeter
than that of Hymettus; come in good courage,
to my structure, for I am pure
of the venom-sending portents, such as that one hides
about the Thracian Neae, whom near to Myrine
the thief of the purple ram dedicated to you, Triple-Father.
26. Dosiadas
The husband of fate-male standing maiden
made me, a mortal twice-grandsire,
not ash-bedded, the son of the spectre, the doom
of the Teucrian herdsman and of the dog's offspring,
the lover of Chrysa, when the man-boiler
shattered the limb-brazen wind,
which the fatherless twice-wedded one,
mother-cast, brought to ruin.
But beholding my fabric
the slayer of Theocritus,
the burner of the thrice-evening one,
cried out and lamented;
for the belly-crawler galled him with venom,
having shed its old age.
And him who ever pours upon the wave-washed shore,
the bedfellow of Pan's mother, the thief,
twice-living, and the son of the man-eater, the destroyers of Ilium,
with their arrows they led to thrice-sacked Troy.

title: Greek Anthology
Greek Anthology
text:
29. Ignatius
Ignatius, having lived amid many transgressions,
have left the light of the sweet-shining sun;
and now I am hidden here in the dark tomb,
alas, my soul long enduring its punishment.
But, O Judge — I am a mortal, and you are deathless and merciful —
be gracious, be gracious to me with kindly eye.
30. Ignatius
On Paul the monk
The body, not the virtue, of good Paul does this tomb
hide beneath it; for like the sun
his most glorious words flash forth with radiance,
and the labours of his virtue hold a great boast.
Twenty years and three he served upon the earth,
and living by reason he received a noble end.
31. Ignatius
On Samuel the deacon of the Great Church
Holy Samuel is hidden in the bosom of the earth,
having left all of life, all that he had, to God;
and now he has run into the bright court of the pious,
to receive glory for his great labours.
32. Arethas
written when he had become archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, upon his own sister
Though swift fate quenched my lamp of life,
robbing me of the light of my torch,
yet the demon was content, in the rage of his malice,
to fill my whole life with grief;
he made me a widow with the babe still lifted to my breast,
nor did I see my fair child playing,
a sweet ornament in the arms of its parents; therefore grief
unbearable subdued me with the fierce
fire of consumption. Three years past twenty
this tomb received me, the host of my
birth; here weave, my parents,
aged, a dirge, tearing your grey hairs,
and the band of well-born brothers groaning, remembering Anna,
gladly recalling the splendour of her beauty.
33. Arethas
On the same woman
The reverend character, the kindly grace,
the obedience of her ways toward her parents
— for modesty led her, like a great teacher,
ever present — the bright tokens of her lineage,
and her loving resolutions against nature
that shook the unsteady with the violence of widowhood,
overcome instead by the entwining of better things;
the radiant garlands from which, according to worth,
the one-husbanded boldness shining forth
of Anna — the tomb shall not be able to dim it.
For the mouth of her shall never escape any,
that bore a fair admonition to life;
and if it should, the inscription shall speak more than all,
this one, set beside the very tomb.
34. Arethas
On Phebronia the nun
Do something even among the spirits of men below,
Phebronia, the tokens of your fellow-feeling,
if there is here any need of the rich for the poor —
for not even there are the souls
of the great-hearted forgetful of their own kindness;
and though the span of our life
be sufficient, may it be God's to send her on to the bridal chamber
of Christ, whom she chose, a holy bride of incorruption,
brightening the lamp with the oil of love for the poor;
of her know this to be the sign of her long sleep.
35. Theophanes the Confessor
Would that I had become a white lily, that with your hands
plucking me, you might rather sate yourself with my flesh.
36. Cometas the Grammarian
Both your tablets, O man of many words, Cometas, beholding,
aged as they were, he has made them ever-flourishing.
37. Cometas the Grammarian
On the poetry of Homer corrected by him
Your books, great-hearted Homer, two of them outright
Cometas, finding them aged, made younger;
for scraping off their age, he showed them most splendid to mortals,
to the wise, in whom there is understanding.
38. Cometas the Grammarian
On the same
Cometas, finding the Homeric books
corrupted and in no way punctuated,
having punctuated them, I worked them over skilfully,
wiping away the rottenness as useless,
and writing, I made the usefulness new again.
From this the copyists, no longer erring,
learn, as it seems, to learn.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
39. Ignatius
On his own works
Ignatius wrought these things, well-skilled in wise song;
Ignatius wrought these things, who brought to light the art
of grammar, hidden in the sea of forgetting.
39A. Ignatius
Having searched out the depths of Plato,
you have torn up the passions of the reasonings.
40. Cometas the Grammarian
When the good son of the All-ruler, leader of men,
who is lord over all mortals and immortals,
spoke to his disciples, the wise fishermen:
"Lazarus, our friend, has left the light of the sun
forever, and now four days dead the boundless earth has hidden him."
But he lay speechless, with lips closed in silence,
his body rotting, and his bones and his fair flesh,
and his soul, flying from his limbs, had gone down to Hades,
and laid upon his friends unspeakable wailing and grief,
and most of all upon Martha and Mary, his kindred,
his own sisters;
for they loved their brother dearly, who lay
in the midst among the dead, lifeless, breathless even so.
Bewailing his fate and mourning they made lament,
sitting outside the tomb, and seated about the grave.
While the sun ran its third day toward the earth,
so long among the dead Lazarus wasted, breathless;
but when the fourth rosy Dawn came,
then the son of the great God spoke
to his beloved well-born friends, who were born of God,
who in counsel surpassed mortals, and surpassed all,
whom he loved exceedingly, as though they were sons of God,
from whose tongue a voice flowed sweeter than honey,
and words like the snowflakes of winter:
"O bright-souled friends, since God is with us,
hear me, all you who hold God within,
that I may tell what my heart in my breast commands me:
come to Bethany, where Lazarus' life-breath left him,
let us hasten with all speed, that I may win undying glory;
for I go to raise our dear friend even from Erebus."
And the noble bright-souled men answered him:
"Let us go, as you command, you who are like to your father."
They spoke; and he himself went on, and led his disciples.
Hastening they followed in the footsteps of the All-ruler,
as go the swarms of thronging bees,
ever coming new from the hollow rock —
so the disciples followed behind the great God.
But when they came to the much-wept tomb,
then the sisters and the kinsfolk, rolling at his feet,
besought Christ the All-ruler:
"We beseech you, lord, who dwell in the highest halls;
Lazarus, whom you loved, has gone into the bowels of Hades;
for had you been here, Aïdoneus, lord of the dead,
would never have endured to wait, since you were far the mightiest;
but even so, if you will, you can raise him again."
And then the Most High answered: "Where does he lie?"
And they swiftly went up the barrow in a body,
and when they had shown God the man and the grievous tomb,
he said: "Set yourselves and lift the lid of the grave."
But when the grievous tomb of the dead man was opened,
then God who is great, and man as well, cried aloud:
"Lazarus, come here, hear me, and come forth."
So when the dead man heard the Word of God speaking,
loose-limbed he rose, bound, breathing, with the smell of death upon him.
And the crowds, seeing him, were amazed in their hearts.
At once they glorified the good God who rules on high,
and the great Father won undying glory for his goodly Son.
41. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Constantine the charioteer
You stood not in bronze while still you lived, Constantine;
for in place of fair fame, envy prevailed.
But when you died, then the whole city honours you
with what it can; yet what is worthy of your horsemanship?

title: Greek Anthology
text:
42. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Since Constantine went down within the house of Hades,
with him departed all the glory of charioteers.
43. Anonymous Epigrammatists
A golden prize in place of merit befitted Constantine,
for the art brought forth no other like him.
As a youth he conquered the famed drivers;
and grown old he showed the young to be feebler.
Whom even after death, by some ever-remembered decree,
the people and the emperor set up in reverence.
44. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Porphyrius the charioteer
Porphyrius, who had ceased from his toils and loosed his band,
and who already stood in bronze in place of merit,
here again they set up in bronze and in silver.
Old man, you who have met with the gifts of strangers,
at the people's shouting you took up the reins again,
and as one twice young you rage in the race-courses.
45. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Julian the charioteer
This Julian, offspring of a Tyrian nurse,
a charioteer who won many crowns,
the emperor himself, and all the people, and the august council
set up, casting a common vote.
For in old age he ceased from the race-courses; and to all he left
a love-charm, in whom flowered the passion for rivals.
46. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Porphyrius the charioteer
This is Porphyrius the Libyan; upon the victorious chariots
he alone won crowns of every kind.
For royal victory, divided among the people,
changed fortunes with colours and with robes;
it fitted him to belong more to the Blues, from whom he rose,
golden in place of merit, bronze in place of toils.
47. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This Porphyrius Libya bore, and Rome reared him,
and victory crowned him in turn, now from one
colour, now another, bearing the tokens of victory on his head.
For often he changed his factions, often his colts;
now first, now last, now in the middle,
he conquered all together, rivals and comrades alike.
48. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Uranius the charioteer
Equal to the glorious — to Faustiniades and to Faustinus
himself — the emperor set Uranius up
beside them both, to whom the people gave, for his measureless victories,
the surname of holy Pelops.
"As ever God leads like to like" —
so one beholding these would speak in truth.
49. Anonymous Epigrammatists
To you alone, both while contending and after you ceased from contests,
Victory gave this prize twice, Uranius,
from both factions; for of old among the Blues
you wear the crown of twenty most glorious years.
You ceased from horsemanship; but the Greens sought you;
to these you gave victory, and they gave you the prize.
50. Anonymous Epigrammatists
You ought to have borne arms, not to carry these robes,
since you are a driver, and a champion of wars.
For when the tyrant-slaying spear-point of the emperor came,
you too, taking up the lance, touched the sea-battle;
and, cunning one, you skilfully seized a double victory,
the one of the horse-race, the other of the tyrant's slaying.
51. Archias
On the Calydonian boar
I am bronze, but behold how great the boldness of the boar
the sculptor achieved, fashioning a living beast,
the mane upon his neck bristling, gnashing his whetted tusk,
sending a fearful gleam from his eyes,
his lips all wetted with foam; no longer is it a marvel
if he destroyed a chosen army of demigods.
1. Damagetus
I am a wrestler neither from Messene nor from Argos;
Sparta, glory of men, is my homeland.
Those are men of art; but I, as befits
the sons of the Lacedaemonians, prevail by force.
2. Simonides
Know, when you behold him, Theognetus the Olympic victor,
the boy, the skilful charioteer of the wrestling-ring,
fairest to look upon, and in the contest no worse than his form,
who crowned the city of his noble fathers.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
3. Simonides
At the Isthmus and at Pytho Diophon, son of Philon, won
the long jump, the foot-race, the discus, the javelin, the wrestling.
4. Anonymous Epigrammatists
What words might Hector speak as he is wounded by the Greeks
Cast now at my body after my death, since even
hares insult the corpse of a dead lion.
5. Alcaeus
Xerxes too led the Persian army to the land of Hellas,
and Titus led one from broad Italy;
but the one came to lay the slave's yoke upon the neck
of Europe, the other to free Hellas from slavery.
6. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The lord of Europe, who both on sea and on dry land
was as much a king over mortals as Zeus over the immortals,
to Hecate of the wayside dedicated the spoils of bold Ciroadas,
and of his children, and of all the Odrysian land,
this son of Demetrius of the goodly ash-spear; but the glory
of Philip has again gone close to the thrones of the gods.
6a. Panteleus
Panteleus
On Callimachus and Cynegirus
O empty toil and fruitless war!
What shall we say to our king of these immortals?
O king, why did you send me against immortal warriors?
We strike, they do not fall; we wound, they do not fear.
One man alone has plundered a whole army; and in their midst
he stands all bloody, the unwearied image of Ares,
he stands like a tree upon iron roots,
and will not fall; but soon he comes, within the ships.
Cast off, helmsman; let us flee the threats of the dead.
7. Alcaeus
Mixing a harmonious sound with the soft pipes,
Dorotheus breathed out the woes of the Dardanians,
and the thunder-pang of Semele's labour, and he breathed the deeds
of the horse, touching the ever-living Graces;
he alone, among the prophets of holy Dionysus,
escaped the swift wings of blame,
a Theban by birth, son of Sosicles; and in the temple
of Lyaeus he set up his mouth-band and his reeds.
8. Alcaeus
No more upon pine-nurturing Phrygia, as once, will you play,
sounding your strain through the well-bored reeds,
nor any more in your hands shall the work of Tritonian Athena,
as before, blossom forth, nymph-born Satyr.
For now your hands are bound in inescapable fetters, because, a mortal,
you matched yourself against Phoebus in a divine contest.
And the pipes, sounding sweet as the lyre,
gave you from the contest not a crown, but death.
9. Anonymous Epigrammatists
O belly, you dog-fly, through whom flatterers and parasites
sell the law of freedom for a bowl of broth.
10. . . .
11. Hermocreon
Sit beneath this shady plane-tree, stranger, as you pass by,
whose leaves Zephyrus stirs with his gentle breath,
where Nicagoras set me up, glorious Hermes son of Maia,
guardian of the fruitful field and of its goods.
12. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Come, and sit beneath my pine, which, leaning toward the soft
west winds, makes its honeyed murmur;
behold too the honey-dripping spring, where, piping,
I bring sweet sleep with my lonely reeds.
13. Plato
Sit beside this lofty, vocal pine
that shivers its cone beneath the thick west winds,
and beside my plashing streams the pipe
shall bring deep slumber upon your charmed eyelids.
14. Zenodotus
Who carved Love and set him beside the fountains,
thinking to quench this fire with water?
15. Anonymous Epigrammatists
He who once was ever drunk with the wine-spring of Bromius,
the goat-footed Satyr, companion of the revellers,
bound in fetters about his double legs,
forges arms for the child of the goddess Thetis,
plying no skilful work of his craft, but rescuing
