a poor livelihood from his toils.
15a. Anonymous Epigrammatists

title: Greek Anthology
text:
a. Where are those cups of yours, glutton? Where the fair
frames of the thyrsus, and the revels, leaping-footed Satyr?
Who fastened upon you, near the carving-knives, the foot-binding band,
and set you, who once swathed yourself in the swaddling-clothes of Bromius?
b. Unseemly want, and all-daring necessity,
which set me beside Hephaestus, a drinker of cinders.
16. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Everything in excess is unfitting; for there is an old saying,
that even of honey the surplus turns to gall.
17. Anonymous Epigrammatists
O Pan, sound the holy strain for the feeding flocks,
sending your curved lip over the golden reeds,
that the goats may carry to the house of Clymenus
their udders heavy with the gifts of white milk,
and that for you the husband of the she-goats, standing fairly at your altars,
may belch crimson blood from his shaggy breast.
18. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Delight your mind by borrowing; but to the moneylenders
leave the finger-bending pain of counting their pebbles.
19. Anonymous Epigrammatists
"Peace to all," said the bishop as he came in.
How can he give to all what he alone holds within?
19a. Herodicus
Flee, you followers of Aristarchus, over the broad back of the sea,
flee Hellas, more cowardly than the tawny fawn,
corner-buzzers, monosyllable-men, who care
for their sphin and sphoin, and the min and the nin.
Let this be your portion, you blustering ones; but for Herodicus
may Hellas ever remain, and god-born Babylon.
20. Palladas
When I saw the orator Maurus, the thick-lipped,
I marvelled at him, the white-robed demon of the rhetorical art.
21. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Nicholas, Patriarch of Alexandria
He who subdued kings and stilled the violence
of his adversaries, for the sake of his fathers' good order,
he lies beneath this small monument,
having become Nicholas, high priest of Christ.
But his virtue, rich in blessings, flew to the ends of the world,
and his soul attends the chambers of the blessed.
For such a life he longed while he was upon the earth,
oppressing his fair body with glorious toils.
22. Anonymous Epigrammatists
A pillar of good order and an offering of temperance,
the image of Nicholas Gregory set up.
23. Simonides
a. Tell me, who are you, whose son, of what homeland, and what do you win?
b. Casmylus, son of Evagoras, in the Pythian boxing, a Rhodian.
24. Simonides
This is the fair statue of fair Milon, who at Pisa
seven times won, and never fell upon his knees.
25. Philippus
If you have heard of Damostratus of Sinope,
who took the Isthmian pine six times,
this is the man you behold; in the well-rounded wrestling-bout
his back, when fallen, never set its seal upon the sand.
Look at his face, fierce as a beast's, and see how still
it keeps the old rivalry for victory.
And the bronze says: "Let the base release me,
that I, breathing, may now grapple in the dust a seventh time."
26. Simonides
We were subdued beneath the fold of Dirphys; and over us
a public monument has been heaped near the Euripus,
not unjustly; for we lost our lovely youth,
when we met the rough storm-cloud of war.
26a. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Uranius
His are the valour and the glory throughout Hellas, who many a work
wrought, in other ways and in counsels both,
the Arcadian spearman Philopoemen, on whom great glory
followed in war, a leader of the spear;
the trophies wrought tell of the twin tyrants
of Sparta; and he lifted off the slavery as it grew.
For which Tegea set up the high-souled son of Craugis,
the achiever of blameless freedom.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
26b. Philippus
Of the king of the Macedonians
Barkless and leafless, traveller, upon this height
a sheer cross is fixed for Alcaeus.
27. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Sardanapalus
Knowing well that you are mortal, increase your spirit's joy,
delighting in feasts; for the dead have no profit.
For I too am ashes, who reigned over great Nineveh.
I have only what I ate and what I insulted, and what with love
I enjoyed; but all those many blessed things are left behind.
This is the wise counsel of life for men.
28. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Hellas judged the Thebans of old the best at the pipes;
and the Thebans judged Pronomus, the son of Oeniades.
29. Anonymous Epigrammatists
If ever you have heard of a dear son of Enyalius,
both mighty in strength and bold to make war,
know that Hector, son of Priam, was the only such man born,
whom once, as he fought, the hero Diomedes slew —
Ajax, offering battle to the Danaans before the Trojans;
him too, dead, this tomb here covers round.
30. Tullius Geminus
The hand of Polygnotus of Thasos made me; and I am that
Salmoneus, who raged against the thunders of Zeus,
who plunders me even in Hades again, and casts at me
with thunderbolts, hating my speechless likeness.
Hold your lightning, Zeus, lay aside your anger; for I am breathless,
a mere mark; do not war with soulless images.
31. Speusippus
The body of Plato earth holds here in her bosom;
but his soul has the godlike rank of the blessed.
32. Leontius Minotaurus
On the image of Gabrielius the prefect in Byzantium
Even Phaethon has his likeness drawn by the pencil; but art carves
the sun, when its rays are hidden,
and you too, wise city-ruler Gabrielius, art draws,
yet short of your virtues, short of all your toils.
32a. Theaetetus
This is Julian, the light of the law, said Rome and Beroe,
when they beheld him; nature can do all things.
33. Leontius Minotaurus
On the image of Callinicus the chamberlain
In beauty you conquer the heart as much as the eye;
for you bear all things worthy of your name.
Ever in the chambers, lulling the emperor to rest,
you sow gentleness into every ear.
34. Theodoretus
On the image of Philip, governor of Smyrna
From Philadelphia these gifts of hospitality to Philip.
Consider how mindful the city is of good government.
35. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The Carians are mindful of their many benefactions,
admiring Palmas the upright judge so greatly.
36. Agathias Scholasticus
On the image of a certain sophist in Pergamum
The images owed long ago for your tales and your nimble
honeyed song — may you forgive their delay;
but now for your sweat and your care for the city
we have set you up, Heraclamon, with this pencil.
And if the gift is small, do not blame it; for with such things
we ever requite good men.
37. Leontius Minotaurus
You see Peter in golden robes; and beside him
the magistracies are witnesses of his alternating toils:
the first office of the East, and the second after it,
of the purple shellfish, and again of the East.
38. Joannes Barbucallus
On the image of Synesius the advocate, set up in Berytus on his victory in a contest
Not only by the Eurotas are there men who are warriors,
nor only by the Ilissus are there men mindful of justice;
as one from Sparta, as a citizen of Athens herself,
Synesius — Victory and Justice admired him.
39. Arabius
On the image of Longinus the prefect in Byzantium
The Nile, Persia, Iberia, the Solymi, the West, Armenia, the Indians,
and the Colchians near the Caucasian crags,
and the plains seething with the far-scattered Agarenes
are witnesses of Longinus' swift labours,
how swiftly he went as the emperor's messenger,
and swiftly bestowed the peace that had been hidden.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
40. Crinagoras
Not three Fortunes alone, Crispus, would it have befitted
to be your neighbours, for the sake of your deep-rich heart,
but all the Fortunes of all men; for what would suffice
so great a man, for the boundless joy of his friends?
But now may Caesar, greater even than these, raise you up
to greater things. What fortune holds firm without him?
41. Agathias Scholasticus
On an image set up in the building of Placidia by the men of the new office
Thomas, the blameless guardian of the universal sovereign,
they set up who serve the new order,
close to the divine pair, that even by his image
he might have a place neighbouring the empire.
For he himself raised on high the thrones of the holy hall,
increasing wealth, but with piety.
Right-minded is the work; for what can the pencil bestow,
save the remembrance owed to good men?
42. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The great Theodosius, leader of Asia, mighty in counsel,
we set up in marble as proconsul,
because he raised Smyrna and brought her again to light,
much sung for her wondrous works.
43. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Damocharis, far-famed and wise judge, yours is this glory,
that Smyrna, after the deadly afflictions of the earthquake,
toiling eagerly, you brought to completion once again.
44. Anonymous Epigrammatists
All nature, O queen, ever sings your power,
because you destroyed the ranks of the enemy, because you kindled
light for temperate men after evil strife,
and scattered the kindred woes of the Amazon's battle.
45. Anonymous Epigrammatists
We orators were minded, joining together,
to honour Theodorus with golden, ever-remembered pencils,
had he not fled gold, even gold within the pencils.
46. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Nicetas, daring with the spear, the emperor, the army, the cities, the people
set up, for his great Mede-slaying toils.
47. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The great in wars, the fearless leader,
Nicetas, the Greens set up for his valour.
48. Anonymous Epigrammatists
I am Proclus, son of Paul, a Byzantine, whom, flourishing
about the house of Justice, the royal court carried off,
that I might be the faithful mouth of the mighty emperor.
This bronze proclaims how great is the prize of contests.
And all things are alike, both for the son and for the father;
but among the consuls' rods the son surpassed his sire.
49. Apollonides
Time of old marvelled at Cinyras, or at both the Phrygians;
but your beauty, Leon, we will sing,
far-famed son of Cercaphus; and the most blessed of islands
is Rhodes too, which shines with such a sun.
50. Apollonides
If such a Leon had been matched against Heracles,
this would not have been the twelfth of the labours of Alcides.
51. Macedonius II
I set up the boy Thyonichus in the statue, not that you may behold
how fair he is in the splendour of this monument,
but that you, learning the contest he toiled through,
my good friend, may feel the same ardour of that same passion.
This is he who never bent his foot in weariness, but in every contest
conquered his equal, the younger and the elder.
52. Philippus
Perhaps, beholding me, stranger, bull-bellied
and stiff-limbed, like a second Atlas,
you wonder, disbelieving that my nature is mortal.
But know me, Heras of Laodicea, the all-wrestler,
whom Smyrna crowned, and the oaks of Pergamum,
Delphi, Corinth, Elis, Argos, Actium;
and if you search out my mastery in the rest of the contests,
you will number even the Libyan sand.
53. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Whether Ladas leapt the stadium or flew across it,
his speed is divine, beyond all telling.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
54. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Such as you were, breathing Ladas, fleeing the wind-swift
Thymus, poised upon your toetip's utmost breath,
such did Myron forge you, stamping upon all your
body the expectation of the Pisan crown.
54a. Anonymous Epigrammatists
He is full of hope, and on the edge of his lips the panting breath
shows from within the hollow of his flanks.
Soon the bronze will leap for the crown, nor will the base
hold it back. O art, swifter than breath!
55. Troilus
a. Image, who set you up, for whose sake, or to whom? Tell me.
b. In return for wrestling the city set me up for Lyron.
56. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This image to Eusebius the Byzantine Rome gave,
beside two others, for his horsemanship.
For not as one who won a disputed victory was he crowned,
but prevailing greatly by his feet and his manhood.
Therefore he quenched the strife of his rivals; but he also stopped
the people's former dissension.
57. Paulus Silentiarius
On a Bacchant in Byzantium
Not nature but art made the Bacchant frenzied,
and mingled madness into the stone.
58. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Hold back the Bacchant, lest, stone though she is,
crossing the threshold, she rush out of the temple.
59. Agathias Scholasticus
On the same
The sculptor set up a Bacchant who did not yet
know how to shake the cymbals in her hands, all modest;
for so she leans forward; and she seems to cry out this:
"Go forth! And I will clash, when no one stands by."
60. Simonides
a. Who is this? b. A Bacchant. a. And who carved her? b. Scopas.
a. And who drove her mad, Bacchus or Scopas? b. Scopas.
61. Crinagoras
Risings and settings, the measures of the world; and the deeds of Nero
reached both the ends of the earth through them.
The sun, as it rose, saw Armenia subdued beneath his hands,
and as it set, saw Germany.
Let his double mastery in war be sung; the Araxes knows it,
and the Rhine, drunk by enslaved nations.
62. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of the emperor Justinian in the Hippodrome
These gifts to you, O Mede-slaying emperor, brings
the father and the son of your Rome, Eustathius:
a colt for victory, a crown-bearing Victory besides,
and you seated upon the wind-swift colt.
On high, Justinian, be your power; and on the earth ever
may the bond hold the champions of the Medes and the Scythians.
63. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
The colt together and the king and Babylon perishing
the bronze fashioned from the spoils of the Assyrians.
It is Justinian, whom, drawing the yoke upon the East,
Julian set up, a Mede-slaying witness.
64. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of the emperor Justin in the harbour
This beside the shores I, Theodorus the prefect,
set up, a shining statue, to Justin the emperor,
that even in the harbours he might spread his own calm.
65. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of the emperor Theodosius
You leapt forth from the East, another light-bringing sun,
Theodosius, to mortals, at the centre of the sky, gentle-hearted,
holding the ocean at your feet, beyond the boundless earth,
all-radiant on every side, helmeted, your shining horse
easily, great-hearted, reining in even as he rushes on.
66. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The mighty Byzas and lovely Phidaleia
in one Calliades adorned and dedicated.
67. Anonymous Epigrammatists
I, lovely Phidaleia, was made the wife of Byzas;
and I am the gift of an ox-killing contest.
68. Posidippus
This is the image of Cypris — let us see — or rather of Berenice;
I am in doubt which of the two it more resembles.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
69. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Zeno the king the city-ruler Julian set up;
and Zeno's consort Ariadne, Julian.
70. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Seeing the house of Helicon grown young again
by the glorious toils of Julian the city-ruler,
all-golden it stood before the halls of the Pierians.
71. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The all-renowned glory of Julian, who, after the world
of the Pierians, set up a golden Anastasia.
72. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Another image, for victory and laden with spoils, within Susa
the bold Mede will set up for his king;
another the long-haired host of the Avars will set up beyond the Ister,
having shorn the lock from their squalid heads;
but this one, for the flourishing good order here,
the queenly city set up from a consul's office.
But may you remain steadfast, Byzantine Rome, who have your portion,
having received the divine might of Justin.
73. Anonymous Epigrammatists
He who adorned the throne of the Consuls, whom thrice-prefect
and father the greatest emperors called their own,
golden stands Aurelian; and the work is
of the council, whose troubles he himself willingly stilled.
74. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On a magistrate
Mix a little fear with your gentleness, since even
the buzzing bee herself is armed with a sharp sting.
For without the whip the proud horse is not guided,
nor does the herd of swine obey the herdsman,
until it has heard the sound of his loud-cracking staff.
75. Antipater
A child like to Zeus and Apollo and Ares, son of kings,
the answered prayer of a mother's good childbearing,
all things royal came to you from the Fates, all things perfect;
and you were made the work of poets.
Zeus has the royal sceptre, Ares the spear, and beauty
Phoebus holds; but in you, Cotys, all are gathered together.
76. Synesius
The three Tyndarids: Castor, Helen, Polydeuces.
77. Paulus Silentiarius
The pencil scarcely drew the girl's eyes, nor her hair,
nor the surpassing radiance of her colour.
If anyone can paint a flashing, sun-like gleam,
he will paint the gleam of Theodorias too.
78. Anonymous Epigrammatists
You are a grudging pencil, and you envy those who behold,
hiding the golden curls beneath the snood.
But if you hide beneath the image the consular grace of her consular head,
you have no claim to the rest of her beauty.
Every pencil flatters its forms; but you alone
have stolen from the splendour of Theodorias.
79. Synesius
On his own sister
An image of golden Cypris, or of Stratonice.
80. Agathias Scholasticus
A wanton I was, within Byzantine Rome,
granting bought love to all;
but I am Callirhoe of many arts, whom, stung by love,
Thomas set here with the pencil,
showing how great a longing he holds within; for, like to him,
my heart, like melting wax, melted.
81. Philippus
On the statue of Zeus at Olympia
Either God came down to earth from heaven to show his likeness
to you, Phidias, or you went up to behold the god.
82. Simonides
Chares the Lindian made the Colossus at Rhodes,
eighty cubits high.
83. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Ajax
Ajax of Timomachus more than of your father — art seized
your nature; the painter saw you in your madness,
and his hand raved together with the man, and the mingled
tears blended all the pains of your grief.
84. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Not unskilfully did Cimon paint these things; but on every work
falls blame, which not even the hero Daedalus escaped.
85. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Art destroyed the proof; for it cannot even reveal
to whom she gave her head.
86. Anonymous Epigrammatists

title: Greek Anthology
text:
Guard well, far off, the watchman of Tueprasia.
Such as you see me, O you who come past me,
a fig-wood thing, not worked with the file, nor from red ochre,
but from the self-taught knife of a shepherd . . .
Laugh at me to no good purpose, but beware to harm
the property of Eucleus, lest you laugh a bitter Sardinian laugh.
87. Julianus
I gave the life-bearing torch of skill; and from skill
and from unceasing fire I have the sight of woe.
Truly the race of mortals is ever thankless, if Prometheus,
in return for his good deed, suffers this at the bronze-smiths' hands.
88. Julianus
The book of Homer called him unwearied bronze;
but the sculptor showed him put to the test.
Come, see here Prometheus groaning, come, see the pains
of the bronze tormented, from the inmost recesses of its vitals.
Heracles, be indignant, since, after your quiver,
the son of Iapetus has ceaseless agony.
89. Gaius Cornelius Gallus
On Tantalus engraved on a cup
This is he who once shared the table of the blessed, this is he who often
filled his belly with the nectar-drink,
now longs for a mortal drop; and the grudging
mixture is ever lower than his lip.
"Drink," says the carving, "and learn the mysteries of silence;
we who are rash with the tongue are punished thus."
90. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Squeeze the long serpent-necks, mighty
Heracles; throttle the deep throats of the biting things.
Even from infancy cease from toiling at the wrath
of jealous Hera; know yourself even from the cradle.
For not a bronze-wrought bowl, nor cauldrons,
but the road to the court of Zeus, was your prize.
91. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Behold, much-toiling Heracles, your contests,
which you endured and went to Olympus, the home of the immortals:
Geryon, the famous cattle, the great labour of Augeas,
the colts, Hippolyta, the many-headed snake,
the boar, the howling dog of Chaos, the beast of Nemea,
the birds, the bull, the Maenalian hind.
But now, set upon the heights of the unsacked city
of Pergamum, rescue the great sons of Telephus.
92. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The labours of Heracles
First in Nemea he slew the mighty lion,
second, in Lerna he destroyed the many-necked Hydra.
Third upon these, he killed the Erymanthian boar.
After that, fourth, he hunted the golden-horned hind.
Fifth, he drove away the Stymphalian birds.
Sixth, he brought the shining girdle of the Amazon.
Seventh, he cleaned out the great dung of Augeas.
Eighth, from Crete he drove the fire-breathing bull.
Ninth, from Thrace he led the horses of Diomedes.
Tenth, he brought the cattle of Geryon from Erythea.
Eleventh, he led up Cerberus, the dog, from Hades.
Twelfth, he brought the golden apples to Hellas.
The thirteenth, such a grievous contest he had:
in a single night he united with fifty maidens.
93. Philippus
On the same
I slew the boundless beast of Nemea, I slew the Hydra
and the bull, and I shook off the jaw of the boar;
I dragged off the girdle, I took the colts of Diomedes,
I broke off the golden apples, I caught Geryon;
Augeas learned of me; the hind did not escape; I killed the birds;
I led Cerberus up; I myself hold Olympus.
94. Archias
No more, you tillers and ploughmen of Nemea,
cower at the heavy roar of the bull-devouring lion;
for he has fallen beneath best-fighting Heracles,
his neck throttled by the beast-slaying hands.
Drive out your flocks; may Echo, dweller of the lonely glen,
again hear the lowing.
And you, lion-cloaked one, gird yourself again with the hide,
soothing the wrath of bastard-hating Hera.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
95. Damagetus
From Nemea is the lion, but the stranger is of Argive blood,
far the best of beasts the one, of demigods the other.
They come to the contest, casting at each other
a sidelong glance, both for their own lives.
Father Zeus, but may the man from Argos conquer,
that Nemea may again be open ground for you.
96. Anonymous Epigrammatists
What first, what next in my mind, what last with my eyes
shall I marvel at, of the art, the man, or the hind?
Of these, the one, mounting upon the beast's loin, presses with his knee,
having grasped with his hands the fair-branching horns;
and she, gaping wide and panting with much breath,
shows with her tongue her heart hard pressed.
Heracles, rejoice; the whole hind now blooms,
not in her horns alone, but in the golden art.
97. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Who fashioned the groaning bronze? Who by his art
wrought both toil and boldness in the form?
The image has life; and I pity it as it struggles,
and I shudder at the mighty, bold Heracles;
for he holds Antaeus worn out by his hands,
and, bent over, he too seems to send forth a groan.
98. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Heracles drunk
This man, now weighed down with sleep and with the cup,
once, sober, destroyed the wine-heavy Centaurs.
99. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
This all-subduer, sung among men for his twelve labours
for the sake of his mighty manhood,
heavy with wine after the feast, drags his drunken, stumbling step,
conquered by soft, limb-loosing Bromius.
100. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of King Lysimachus
Seeing the hair and the club and in the eyes the fearless
spirit, and the man's grim brow,
look for the lion-skin on the image; and if you find it,
it is Heracles, but if not, the panel of Lysimachus.
101. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On an image of Heracles
Such as Thiodamas of old met Heracles,
such did the craftsman make the son of Zeus,
dragging the plough-ox and stretching out his club;
but he did not paint the deadly ox-slaughter.
Perhaps he fitted to Thiodamas' lips a wailing voice,
which Heracles, hearing, spares him.
102. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On another image of the same
Such as the son of Cronus begot you on that thrice-mooned
night, and Eurystheus saw you crown-bearing,
and from the fire you revelled up to Olympus, O heavy-toiling
Alcides — such an image of you we behold.
The stone holds the birth-pangs of Alcmena; and proud
Thebes now is more incredible than the tales.
103. Tullius Geminus
On a statue of the same
Heracles, where is your great club, and the Nemean
cloak, and the quiver full of arrows?
Where the haughty roar? Why did Lysippus mould you so downcast,
and mingle anguish into the bronze?
You are grieved, stripped of your arms; and who has sacked you?
The winged one, truly one heavy labour, Love.
104. Philippus
On the same
This, then, was all that Hera wished, after all your labours:
to see bold Heracles stripped of his arms.
Where is the lion-cloak, and the swift-whistling arrow upon the shoulders,
and the heavy-footed, beast-slaying branch?
Love has stripped you of all; and no wonder, if, having made Zeus
a swan, he robbed Heracles of his arms.
105. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Theseus and the Marathonian bull
A marvel of art, both bull and man, of whom the one in strength
weighs the beast down by force, straining his limbs,
and bending the neck-sinews, seized with his hands,
with the left the nostrils, with the right the horn,
and wrenched the joints; and the beast, his neck subdued
beneath the mighty hands, sank back behind.
And one may fancy, under the art, in this bronze
that the beast breathes and the man runs with sweat.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
106. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Capaneus
If such a Capaneus
raged against the towers of Thebes,
contriving an airy ascent by ladder,
he would have taken the city by force, even beyond
his fate. For even the thunderbolt
of the son of Cronus was ashamed
to take such a champion.
107. Julianus
On a bronze Icarus standing in a bath
Icarus, wax destroyed you; but now
with wax
the bronze-smith has brought you back to your form again.
But do not shake your wings in the air,
lest, falling from the sky,
you turn the bath into an Icarian sea.
108. Julianus
On the same
Icarus, remember that you are bronze; and let not art deceive you,
nor the pair of wings upon your shoulders.
For if, while living, you fell into the depths of the sea,
how do you wish to fly, having a form of bronze?
109. Agathias Scholasticus
On Hippolytus conversing with Phaedra's nurse
Hippolytus into the old woman's ear speaks
a pitiless word;
but we cannot hear it.
Yet, as far as one can tell from his frenzied eye,
it is plain that he charges her to speak no more lawless things.
110. Flavius Philostratus
On the image of the wounded Telephus
This is the irresistible champion of Teuthrania, this is he who once,
Telephus, bloodied the dreadful war of the Danaans,
when he mingled the Caïcus, Mysian, full of slaughter;
this is the rival of the Pelian spear,
now hiding in his thigh a deadly burden, like one breathless
he wastes away, dragged down with his living flesh.
At whose suffering the Achaeans, crouching in fear,
flee in confusion from the Teuthranian shore.
111. Glaucus
On the image of Philoctetes
Seeing the much-suffering hero from Trachis,
this Philoctetes Parrhasius painted;
for in his hardened eyes there dwells a mute
tear, and the wasting pain is within.
O best of painters, you are skilful; but it was time now
to give the much-toiling man rest from his pains.
112. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
My painter is more an enemy to me than the Danaans, a second Odysseus,
who reminded me of my evil, accursed disease.
The rock, the rags, the gore, the wound, the grief were not enough;
but even in bronze he wrought my pain.
113. Julianus
On the same
I know, looking on Philoctetes, that to all he shows
his suffering, even to those who behold from afar.
He has wild, shaggy hair; come, see the locks
of his head, squalid with their rough colours;
he bears a hardened skin, shrunken to behold,
and perhaps dry to the touch of the hands;
and tears, frozen beneath his dry eyelids,
stand fast, the sign of sleepless misery.
114. Cosmas Indicopleustes
On Pyrrhus about to slay Polyxena
I am Pyrrhus; and I hasten for my father's sake; but the shameless one
calls upon Pallas, having Paris as her brother.
115. Flavius Claudius Julianus the Emperor
On Chiron the horse-Centaur
From the man flows the horse; and from the horse the man runs up,
a man without feet, and headless the dappled horse;
the horse belches out the man, and the man breaks wind into a horse.
116. Euodus
On the same
A headless horse lay there, and an unfinished man,
whom Nature, in her play, grafted onto the swift horse.
117. Cornelius Long(in)us
On Cynegirus
Not you, blessed Cynegirus, did Phasis paint as Cynegirus,
since he set you up with mighty hands;
but the painter was some wise man, and did not deprive
of his hands you, who for your hands' sake are immortal.
118. Paulus Silentiarius
On the same
The Mede-slaying hands above the curved stern
of the ship as it set off the choppers cut away,
when, Cynegirus, that fleeing cargo-ship
clung, as from your moorings, to your hands.
But even so, gripping fast the ship's timber, biting it round,
breathless they followed as a terror to the Persians;
and one barbarian took the ship; but the victory of the hands
remained with the dwellers of Mopsopia.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
119. Posidippus
On the statue of Alexander the Macedonian
Lysippus, Sicyonian sculptor, bold hand,
fiery craftsman, the bronze you cast looks like fire,
the bronze you poured into the form of Alexander. No longer are the Persians
to be blamed: there is forgiveness for cattle that flee a lion.
120. Archelaus
On the same
Lysippus moulded the daring of Alexander and his whole form;
what power has this bronze!
The bronze man seems about to speak, looking up to Zeus:
"I set the earth beneath me; you, Zeus, keep Olympus."
121. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Take this to be Alexander himself; such are his eyes,
and the bronze holds living daring,
who alone, of all that the beams of Zeus look down upon from the sky,
subjected the whole earth to the Pellaean throne.
122. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
This Alexander, son of great-hearted Philip,
you behold newly born, whom once his mother Olympias
bore, strong-spirited; and from the birth-pangs Ares
taught him the works of battle, and Fortune bade him reign.
123. Anonymous Epigrammatists
No longer for ox-feasting Heracles, you country lads,
no longer are these places open to crafty wolves,
and thieves will refuse to walk the road of theft,
even if uncritical sleep should hold the villagers.
For Dionysius set me up, not without a prayer,
in this place, Heracles the good ally.
124. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Do not tremble, traveller, because I have a bow, and have stripped bare
newly-whetted arrows, and set them before my feet,
nor because I bear a club in my hand, nor because I have
this skin of the bright-eyed lion about my shoulders;
I do not know how to harm all men, but only evildoers,
and I am able to save the good from their griefs.
125. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Ever heavy upon the son of Laertes is the sea; a flood
washed away his image, and effaced the likeness from the tablets.
What of it? For in the verses of Homer his
image is written upon imperishable pages.
126. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the Minotaur
The boy-bull, in nothing complete,
the accuser of his mother's passion,
the half-beast man, the double nature,
the bull-headed, the wandering of bodies,
who is neither wholly ox nor wholly man.
127. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Who moulded this Thracian, the single-sandalled Lycurgus,
in bronze, the lord of the Edonians?
Beside the vine-stock, see how, raging proudly,
he raises the heavy iron over his head.
The form reveals the old boldness; and the proud
madness, even in bronze, keeps that bitterness.
128. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Iphigenia
Iphigenia rages; but again the sight of Orestes
leads her back to the sweet memory of kinship;
and as she is angered and yet looks upon her brother,
her glance is drawn out at once with pity and with madness.
129. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Niobe
From life the gods made me stone; but from
stone
Praxiteles wrought me back to life again.
130. Julianus
On the same
You behold the all-true form of wretched Niobe,
as if she still mourned the doom of her children.
But if she did not receive a soul, do not for this
blame the art: she likened a stone to a woman.
131. Antipater
On the same
This daughter of Tantalus, who once bore twice seven children
from a single womb, a sacrifice to Phoebus and to Artemis;
for the daughter sent slaughter upon the girls, the son upon the boys;
the two killed the two sevens.
And she, the mother once of so many flocks, once blessed in children,
wretched, was left not even with one to tend her age;
and a mother, not by her children, as is right, but the children
by their mother, were all led to grievous tombs.
Tantalus, the tongue destroyed you too, and your daughter;
and she was turned to stone, and over you a stone hangs in dread.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
132. Theodoridas
On the same
Stand near, weep when you see, stranger, the countless griefs
of Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, of the unbridled tongue,
whose twelve-child brood she laid upon the earth
just now, some by the bow of Phoebus, some of Artemis.
And she, having a form mingled of stone and flesh,
turns to rock; and high-fixed Sipylus groans.
A treacherous disease for mortals is the tongue, whose unbridled
folly often breeds misfortune.
133. Antipater
On the same
Why, woman, have you raised your shameless hand to Olympus,
casting the god-filled hair from your godless head?
Beholding the great wrath of Leto, O child-rich one,
now lament the bitter and self-willed strife.
For one of your children gasps beside you; another, breathless,
lies fallen; and over another heavy doom hangs.
And this is not yet the end of your toils, but the male
swarm of your children too is laid low, perished.
O you who wept bitterly at the births, you yourself, breathless,
shall be a stone, Niobe, worn down by grief.
134. Meleager
On the same
Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, hear my word, the messenger of ruin;
receive the most piteous tale of your woes.
Loose the band of your hair; alas, you who bore a male brood
for the grievous bows of Phoebus.
Your children are no more. But what is this other thing? What do I see?
Alas, alas, slaughter floods over the maidens.
For one is fallen at her mother's knees, another in her lap,
another upon the earth, another at the breast;
another stares in terror at the facing shaft; another cowers
beneath the arrows; and another's living eye still sees the light.
And the mother, who once loved her chattering mouth, now, in amazement,
flesh-fixed, has hardened like a stone.
135. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Medea in Rome
The art of Timomachus mingled love
and jealousy
in Medea, as her children are dragged to their doom.
For toward the one she leans the sword, but from the other she draws back,
willing both to save and to slay her children.
136. Antiphilus
On the same
When the hand of Timomachus painted deadly Medea,
drawn in opposite ways by jealousy and her children,
it took on countless toil, that it might carve two characters,
of which the one inclined to wrath, the other to pity.
Both he fulfilled; behold the likeness; for in the threat there is
a tear, and in the pity wrath wells up.
"The intent suffices," said the wise man; but the children's blood
befitted Medea, not the hand of Timomachus.
137. Philippus
On the same
Who painted, lawless Colchian, your spirit into the image?
Who wrought a barbarian even in a likeness?
Do you ever thirst for the slaughter of infants? Is some second Jason,
or some Glauce, again your pretext?
Begone, you child-killer, even in the wax. For of your measureless
jealousies even the pencil is aware to what you would do.
138. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Come, see the child-slayer in the image, come, see the statue,
the Colchian, fashioned by the hand of Timomachus:
the sword in her hand, her great fury, her wild eye,
the tear falling upon the most piteous children;
all things at once he poured together, gathering the most unmixed into one,
sparing his hand from staining it with blood.
139. Julianus
On the same
When Timomachus painted Medea, in the image of a lifeless
form he set two souls;
for joining the jealousy over the marriage-bed and the love for her children together,
he showed her in her eyes drawn in opposite ways.
140. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Come, see, and marvel at the pity that lies beneath the brows
and the wrath, and the fiery rim of the eyelids,
and the hand of the mother and wife, bitterly suffering,
drawn with sparing impulse toward the murder.
The painter wisely hid the end of the murder, unwilling
to dull the wonder with grief for the beholders.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
141. Philippus
On the same
The Colchian, the avenging fury over her children, you lisping swallow,
how did you dare to keep as nurse of your own children?
Whose blood-shot eye still flashes murderous fire,
and the grey foam drips from her jaws,
and the iron is newly drenched with blood. Flee the all-destroying
mother, who, even in wax, is still slaying her children.
142. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of the same
You rage even though you are stone, and from your heart your fury,
hollowing your eyes, has made them ready for wrath.
Yet not even the base will hold you, but in your fury
you will leap, raging for your children's sake.
O who was the craftsman that moulded this, or who the sculptor,
who by his skill led stone into madness?
143. Antipater
On the same
This is the likeness of Medea; see how the one eye she raises
to wrath, the other breaks down into pity for her children.
144. Arabius
On Atalanta and Hippomenes
Did you cast bridal gifts, or a delaying of her speed,
this golden prize for the girl, Hippomenes?
The apple accomplished both, since it both checked the maiden's rush,
and was the token of yoking Cypris.
145. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Ariadne
No mortal is the sculptor; but such as
Bacchus your lover
saw you, he carved you reclining upon the rock.
146. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Strangers, do not touch the stone Ariadne,
lest she leap up, seeking Theseus.
147. Antiphilus
On Andromeda
The land is of the Ethiopians; and the one with winged sandals
is Perseus; and she bound to the rock is Andromeda;
the head is of the stone-glaring Gorgon; the prize of love,
the sea-monster; and the chattering proof of Cassiope's fair offspring;
and she loosens her feet from the crag, dull with their wonted
numbness; and the suitor weds the prize.
148. Arabius
On the same
Did Cepheus set Andromeda upon the rocks, or the painter?
For from the eyes the judgement is doubtful.
And was the sea-monster carved upon the bent crags,
or did it rise from neighbouring Nereus?
I know that some wise man wrought these things; truly skilled
he wrought, and wrought a deceit of the wits.
149. Arabius
On the image of Helen
The lovely likeness of Argive Helen, whom once a herdsman
carried off, thrusting aside Zeus the god of strangers.
150. Pollianus
This is the Polyxena of Polycleitus, nor did any other
hand touch this divine panel.
It is the sister-work of Hera. See how, with her robe rent,
she hides her bared modesty with a chaste veil;
the wretched one pleads for her life; and in the eyes
of the maiden lies the whole war of the Phrygians.
151. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Dido
You behold the original of glorious Dido, stranger,
an image shining with divine beauty.
Such indeed I was; but I had not the mind, such as you hear,
having won my fame on honourable grounds.
For I never set eyes on Aeneas, nor in the time
of Troy's sacking did I come to Libya;
but, fleeing the violence of Iarbas' marriage,
I drove the two-edged sword into my heart.
Pierians, why did you arm holy Maro against me,
who lied so against my chastity?
152. Gauradas
Dear Echo, agree with me in something. — In what?
I love a girl; but she does not love me. — She loves you.
And the moment does not bring the chance to act. — It brings it.
Then you, tell her that I love her. — I love her.
And give her some pledge of money. — Give it.
Echo, what remains, but to win my desire? — To win it.
153. Satyrus
On the statue of Echo
Through the shepherd's meadow tongueless Echo sings,
answering the birds with her late-following voice.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
154. Archias
On the same
You see rocky Echo, friend, companion of Pan,
the answering voice that sings back in reverse,
the chattering image of all manner of mouths, a sweet plaything
for shepherds. Whatever you say, hearing this, go away.
155. Euodus
On the same
Echo, the mimic of speech, the dregs of the voice, the tail of a word.
156. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
I am an Arcadian goddess, and I dwell beside the doors of Lyaeus,
answering the spoken word;
for no longer do I hate, dear Bacchus, your reveller;
come, Pan, let us speak our words together.
157. Julianus
On the armed Athena in Athens
Why, Tritogeneia, are you helmeted in the midst of the city?
Poseidon has yielded; spare the land of Cecrops.
158. Diotimus
As is fitting, I am Artemis; and the bronze itself well declares
Artemis the daughter of Zeus, and of no other.
Reckon the boldness of the maiden. Truly you might say:
"All the earth is too small a hunting-ground for her."
159. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Aphrodite in Cnidus
Who gave soul to the stone? Who saw Cypris
upon the earth?
Who wrought such desire in the rock?
This is the work of Praxiteles' hands, surely, or perhaps Olympus
is widowed, since the Paphian has come to Cnidus.
160. Plato
On the same
The Paphian Cytherea came through the waves to Cnidus,
wishing to behold her own image;
and gazing all about in the conspicuous place,
she cried: "Where did Praxiteles see me naked?"
Praxiteles saw not what was unlawful; but the iron
carved her as Ares would have wished the Paphian.
161. Plato
Neither Praxiteles fashioned you, nor the iron;
but you stood thus, just as once when you were judged.
162. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Cypris, when she saw Cypris in Cnidus, said:
"Alas, alas! Where did Praxiteles see me naked?"
163. Pseudo-Lucianus
No one has seen the Paphian naked; but if anyone has seen her,
it is this man who set up the naked Paphian.
164. Pseudo-Lucianus
To you I dedicated the most beautiful image of your form,
Cypris, having nothing finer than your form.
165. Euenus
Pallas and the consort of the son of Cronus said, when they saw
the Cnidian: "We blame the Phrygian unjustly."
166. Euenus
Before, on the Idaean hills, the herdsman himself
beheld her who first bore off the prize of beauty;
but Praxiteles set her, all-visible, before the Cnidians,
holding the vote of Paris as witness of his art.
167. Antipater
You will say, beholding Cypris on rugged Cnidus,
that, stone though she is, she will set even stone afire;
but seeing the sweet Eros of desire among the Thespians,
that he will cast fire even into cold adamant.
Such gods Praxiteles wrought, one in one land
and one in another, that all might not be scorched with double fire.
168. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Paris saw me naked, and Anchises, and Adonis;
those three alone I know; but Praxiteles, whence?
169. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same, and on the Athena in Athens
Look round on the sacred beauty of the foam-born Paphian,
and you will say: "I praise the Phrygian for his judgement."
Looking again at the Attic Pallas, you will cry this:
"How did the herdsman Paris pass her by?"
170. Hermodorus
On the same
Seeing the Cnidian Cytherea, stranger, you would say this:
"She herself rules both mortals and immortals."
But seeing in the city of Cecrops the spear-bold Pallas,
you will declare: "Truly Paris was a herdsman."
171. Leonidas
On Aphrodite armed
These arms of Ares, for what reason, O Cytherea,
have you put on, bearing this empty weight?
For naked you disarmed Ares himself; and if even a god
is undone, in vain you bring arms against men.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
172. Alexander
Pallas herself, surely, perfected Cypris,
forgetting the judgement upon Alexander.
173. Julianus
On the armed Aphrodite in Sparta
Always Cytherea has learned to bear the quiver,
the bow, and the work of the long-range shaft;
but, respecting the laws of war-steadfast Lycurgus,
she brings to Sparta her love-charms in close-fighting arms.
And you in your chambers, Spartan women, revering the arms
of Cythera, bring forth bold children.
174. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Pallas, when she saw Cytherea armed,
said:
"Cypris, will you have us thus go to the judgement?"
And she, laughing gently: "Why should I
lift a shield against you?"
175. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Either the Paphian, stone as she is, armed herself, or rather, perhaps,
the Paphian saw the stone, and swore she wished to be it.
176. Antipater
Cypris too is in Sparta; not as in other cities
is she set up, clothed in soft folds;
but on her head she has a helmet instead of a veil,
and instead of golden boughs a spear-shaft.
For the consort of Thracian Enyalius and a Lacedaemonian
should not be without arms.
177. Philippus
Smile-loving Cypris, tender of the bridal chamber, who crowned you,
the honeyed deity, with the arms of war?
Dear to you was the paean, and golden-haired Hymenaeus,
and the sweet-singing graces of the clear pipes.
Why have you put on these man-killing arms? Do you boast,
having despoiled bold Ares, how much Cypris can do?
178. Antipater
On the same, rising from the sea
The Cypris but now rising from her mother the sea,
behold the labour of Apelles' pencil,
how, gathering her sea-soaked hair with her hand,
she wrings the foam from her wet locks.
179. Archias
On the same
Apelles saw Cypris herself, naked, being born
from the sea, her nurse,
and fashioned her thus, drenched with the water's foam,
still wringing her locks with her blooming hands.
180. Democritus
On the same
When Cypris, her hair dripping with the brine-flowing foam,
naked rose from the purple wave,
thus, surely, taking her tresses in her hands by her white cheeks,
she squeezed out the Aegean sea,
showing her breast alone, which is lawful; but if such
is she, let the spirit of Enyalius be confounded.
181. Julianus
On the same
But now the Paphian rose forth from her sea-birth,
finding the hand of Apelles for her midwife.
But withdraw quickly from the pencils, lest the foam
dripping from her wrung locks wet you.
If such a Cypris once was made naked for the apple,
unjustly did Pallas ravage Troy.
182. Leonidas
On the same
Her who had escaped from her mother's bosom, still
murmuring with foam, well-bedded Cypris,
Apelles, seeing the most lovely beauty,
fashioned her not painted but alive.
For well with her fingertips she wrings her hair,
and well from her eyes a calm desire shines forth,
and her breast, the herald of her prime, is firm as the quince;
and Athena herself and the consort of Zeus
will say: "O Zeus, we are surpassed in the judgement."
183. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On a statue of Dionysus standing near Athena
a. Tell me, what have you in common with Pallas? For to her belong javelins
and wars, but to you feasts are pleasing.
b. Not rashly, stranger, ask such things about the gods;
know in how many ways I am like this deity.
For mine too is the dear glory of wars; the Indian knows me,
subdued from the eastern Ocean,
and we both ennoble the life of men, she with the olive,
but I with the sweet clusters of the cultivated vine.
And indeed not even for me did my mother endure birth-pangs:
I loosed my father's thigh, she his head.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
184. Antipater
On another statue of the same
As fellow-shieldsman to Italian Piso, Dionysus
I am set up, the guardian of the halls, for good fortune.
"Worthily, O Dionysus, you entered the house." Both befitted:
the hall for Bacchus, and Bromius for the hall.
185. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Dionysus and Heracles
Both from Thebes, and both warriors,
and from Zeus; the one terrible with the thyrsus, the other with the club.
Their pillars stand together; their arms are alike,
the fawnskin to the lion-skin, the cymbals to the clapper.
Hera was a harsh goddess to both. And both, from the earth,
came to the immortals out of the fire.
186. Xenocritus
On the statue of Hermes
Swift Hermes am I called; but in the wrestling-school
do not set me up maimed of hands, nor footless;
or how am I swift? How shall I gesture upright with my hands,
standing orphaned of both for a base?
187. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
A man prayed to a wooden Hermes, and it was wood.
Then, lifting it, he dashed it to the ground; and from it gold
streamed when it broke. Insolence has often brought gain.
188. Nicias
Having my lot in the leaf-shaking, steep mountain of Cyllene,
here I stand, the guardian of the lovely gymnasium,
Hermes; over whom the boys often laid marjoram and hyacinth,
and fresh garlands of violets.
189. Anonymous Epigrammatists
A guardian over the beehives, for the sake of Peristratus, I remain
here, having left the Maenalian slope,
watching for the thief of the bees. But beware
my hand, and the light reach of my countryman's foot.
190. Leonidas
Morichus the goatherd set up Hermes the overseer
as the well-reputed guardian of his flocks.
But, O you that have fed upon the green woodland on the hills,
have no care for the ravenous wolf.
191. Nicaenetus
A turning circle of the potter's wheel moulded me here,
an earthen Hermes, with earthen feet.
I was kneaded of clay; I will not lie. But I loved,
stranger, the ill-fated work of the potters.
192. Anonymous Epigrammatists
O best of men, do not think you behold one of the many
images of Hermes; for I am the work of Scopas.
193. Philippus
a. May I touch the cabbage, Cyllenian? b. No, passer-by.
a. What grudge over vegetables? b. No grudge, but a law,
to keep thieving hands off others' property. a. O strange thing:
Hermes has made a new law, not to steal!
194. Palladas
On the statue of Eros
Someone brought a bronze Eros out of fire into fire,
fitting a frying-pan as a torture for the torturer.
195. Satyrus
On a statue of the same, bound
Who fettered the winged one here, who bound in chains the swift fire?
Who laid hold of the flaming quiver,
and shackled the swift-shooting, all-encircling
hands, binding them to a sturdy column?
These are cold comforts for men. May not this prisoner
himself once have bound that one's heart?
196. Alcaeus
On the same
Who fettered you here, unholily caught, and set you up?
Who bound your hands in a tangle,
and made your face squalid? Where are your swift arrows,
foolish one? Where the bitter, fire-bearing quiver?
In vain, surely, the stone-carver toiled, who bound you, who once
stirred the gods with desire, in this snare.
197. Antipater
On the same
Who bound your hands to the column with inescapable
knots? Who took fire with fire, and guile
with guile?
Foolish one, do not let a tear fall down your sweet
face; for you delight in the tears of young men.
198. Quintus Maecius
On the same
Weep, your hands bound past escape, reckless deity,
weep much, dripping soul-melting tears,
you insulter of temperance, mind-stealer, robber of reason,
winged fire, unseen wound of the soul, Eros.
For mortals your bond is a release from their groans, reckless one;
bound by it, send your prayers to the deaf winds.
And the unguarded fire you kindled in mortals' hearts,
behold now quenched by your own tears.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
199. Crinagoras
On the same
Both weep and groan, your sinews bound together
by your hands, you schemer; such things befit you.
There is none to loose you; do not look up smoothly.
For you yourself wrung from the eyes of others
the tear, and fixing bitter shafts in the heart,
you dripped the venom of inescapable longings,
Eros; and the woes of mortals are laughter to you.
You have suffered such things as you did. Justice is good.
200. Moschus
On Eros ploughing
Laying aside torch and bow, shaggy Eros took up
the ox-driving goad, and had a wallet on his shoulder,
and, yoking the patient necks of bulls beneath the yoke,
he sowed the wheat-bearing furrow of Deo.
And looking up he said to Zeus himself: "Fill the fields,
lest I cast you, the bull of Europa, beneath the plough."
201. Marianus
On Eros crowned
Where is that back-bent bow of yours, and the reeds that,
shot from you, fix themselves in the very heart?
Where are your wings? Where the much-paining torch? And why three
garlands do you hold in your hands, and bear another on your head? —
"Not from the common Cypris, stranger, nor from the earth
am I, nor the offspring of woodland mirth;
but I kindle in the pure mind of men the torch
of good learning, and lead the soul up to heaven.
And from the virtues I weave four crowns; from each of which
bearing these, I am crowned first with that of wisdom."
202. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Do not call me, stranger, the one from Lebanon, the revel-lover
who delights in the night-time talk of young men;
I am a humble countryman from a neighbouring Nymph,
urging on only the works of planting.
Whence from the fruitful, dear vineyard four
garlands of the Seasons crowned me, four in number.
203. Julianus
On the Eros of Praxiteles
Bending his proud neck beneath our sandals,
Praxiteles fashioned me with plundering hands.
For Eros himself, who lies hidden within me,
he forged in bronze, and gave to Phryne as a gift of love;
and she again brought him to Eros; for it is lawful for lovers
to bring Eros himself as a gift to Eros.
204. Simonides
On the same
Praxiteles made exact the Eros that he suffered,
drawing the original from his own heart,
giving me to Phryne as the price of myself. And I breed love-charms
no longer by shooting, but by being gazed upon.
205. Tullius Geminus
On the same
In return for love, Praxiteles gave Eros, a god, to mortal
Phryne, finding both his fee and a god.
And she did not refuse the maker; for her heart feared
lest the god take up allied arms in place of art.
But she no longer dreads the Eros of Cypris, but the one from you,
Praxiteles, knowing art to be his mother.
206. Leonidas
On the same
The Thespians revere Eros as the only god from Cytherea,
painted from no other original,
but the one Praxiteles knew as a god; whom, gazing about Phryne,
he gave as the ransom of his own longings.
207. Palladas
Eros is naked; for this he laughs and is gentle;
for he has no bow nor fiery arrows;
nor in vain does he hold in his hands a dolphin and a flower:
for in the one he holds the earth, in the other the sea.
208. Gabrielius
On Eros sleeping in a bed of pepper
Not even in slumber, nor breathless, nor at a feast
is Eros free from his fire-sown sting.
209. Anonymous Epigrammatists
You who blow upon the brand to light your lamp,
come, light it from my soul; for I am all aflame.
210. Plato
When we came to the deep-shaded grove, we found within
the child of Cythera, like to purple apples.
He had no quiver holding arrows, no curved bow;
but these hung upon the well-leaved trees,
and he himself, fettered in sleep among the rose-cups,
slept smiling; and overhead the tawny bees
sprinkled upon his sweet lips their wax-poured honey.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
211. Statyllius Flaccus
On Eros sleeping
You sleep, bringing sleepless cares upon mortals;
you sleep, ah child of the baneful Foam-born,
not lifting the fiery pine-torch, nor unguarded
plucking the shaft from your counter-stretched bow.
Let others take heart; but I, proud one, am afraid,
lest even in your slumber you see some bitter dream of me.
212. Alpheus
On the same
I shall snatch the fiery torch, Eros, from your hand,
I shall strip the quiver that hangs about your shoulders,
if truly you sleep, offspring of fire, and your men
I lead to a little good order of the bow.
But even so I fear you, schemer, lest you hide some plot
against me, and even in sleep see a bitter dream.
213. Straton
Even if swift wings are stretched about your back,
and Scythian arrow-points dart from your bow,
I shall flee you, Eros, beneath the earth. But what good? For not even
all-subduing Hades himself
escaped your might.
214. Secundus
On statues of Loves
See the spoil-loving Loves, see how upon their sturdy shoulders
they bear the arms of the gods, the babes exulting:
the drums and the thyrsus of Bromius, and the thunderbolt of Zeus,
the shield of Enyalius and his fair-crested helmet,
the well-bowed quiver of Phoebus, the trident of the Sea,
and the club of the strong hands of Heracles.
What more for men, when Eros has even taken the sky,
and Cypris has plundered the arms of the immortals?
215. Philippus
Having despoiled Olympus, see how the Loves
adorn themselves with the arms of the immortals, exulting in their spoils.
They bear the bow of Phoebus, and the thunderbolt of Zeus, the weapon
and helmet of Ares, the club of Heracles,
and the club of the god, the three-barbed spear, and the thyrsus of Bacchus,
the winged sandals of Hermes, the torches of Artemis.
It is no burden for mortals to yield to the shafts of the Loves,
to whom the gods have given the ornament of arms to hold.
216. Parmenion
On the statue of Hera
Argive Polycleitus, who alone
beheld Hera with his eyes
and, having seen all that he saw, fashioned her,
showed her beauty to mortals, as far as is lawful; but the forms
hidden beneath her robe, unknown, are kept for Zeus.
217. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Calliope
I am Calliope; and to Cyrus I gave my breast,
who reared divine Homer, whence sweet Orpheus drank.
218. Joannes Barbucallus
The painter wished to draw Melpomene in the image,
but, falling short, he painted Calliope.
219. Joannes Barbucallus
This image is yours, Polymnia, and yet it is also the Muse's;
for over both there is one name and one likeness.
220. Antipater
On images of the Muses
We three Muses stand here; one bears the pipes,
one in her hands the lyre, and one the tortoise-shell.
The one holds the lyre of Aristocles, the one of Ageladas
the barytone, and the one of Canachas the hymn-singing reeds.
But the one is mistress of the tone, the other the singer
of the melody, and the other the inventor of wise harmony.
221. Theaetetus
On the Nemesis of the Athenians
Me, a snow-white stone, from the ever-growing crag
the Mede, having cut me with stone-cutting points,
carried over the sea, that he might make of me a man's likeness,
the token of his triumph over the Athenians.
But when Marathon clashed back at the slaughtered Persians,
and the ships sailed the watery ways on bloody streams,
the noblest Athens carved me into Adrasteia,
a deity opposed to overweening men.
I weigh hopes against hope; and I am even now
victory for the sons of Erechtheus, Nemesis for the Assyrians.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
222. Parmenion
On the same
Hoped by the Medes to be a trophy-bearing stone,
I was changed in form, fittingly, into Nemesis,
set up, a just goddess, on the banks of Rhamnus,
a witness for Attica of victory and of wisdom.
223. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Nemesis
Nemesis forewarns, by her cubit-rule and by her bridle,
to do nothing beyond measure, nor to speak things unbridled.
224. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
I, Nemesis, hold a cubit-rule; for what reason, you will ask.
I proclaim to all: nothing beyond the measure.
225. Arabius
On the statue of Pan
One might almost have heard distinctly Pan piping,
for the sculptor mingled breath into the figure;
but, seeing wandering Echo flee, helpless, ever-shifting,
he refused the useless note of the pipe.
226. Alcaeus
On the same
Breathe, Pan, with your sweet lips the mountain-ranging Muse,
breathe, delighting in the shepherd's reed,
pouring melody from the tuneful pipe, and from the accompanying
strain ring out, guiding the harmony of the word;
and around you, to the rhythm's beat, let the inspired step
be danced for these water-dwelling Nymphs.
227. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Here, cast down upon the green meadow, traveller,
rest your soft limbs from your weary toil,
where the pine, shaken by the breezes of Zephyrus,
will charm you, as you listen to the cicadas' song;
and the shepherd in the mountains, piping near the spring at midday,
beneath the shade of a leafy plane-tree;
and, fleeing the heat of the autumn Dog-star, you will cross the height
in season. Heed Hermes, who tells you this.
228. Anyte
Stranger, rest your wearied limbs beneath the elm;
sweetly the breeze murmurs in the green leaves;
and drink the cool spring-water from the fountain; for to travellers
this is a welcome rest in the hot heat.
229. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Pan
This dearest one is poured forth from Zeus himself;
and the cloud above bears witness.
For cloud-gathering Zeus begot lord Hermes;
and Hermes begot Pan the goat-driver.
230. Leonidas
Do not, traveller, drink here this warm water of the gully,
full of mud from the sheep-pasture;
but go a little beyond this heifer-grazed
height, there, beside that shepherd's pine,
and you will find, gurgling through the fair-fountained rock,
a stream colder than the northern snow.
231. Anyte
a. Why, Pan the hunter, sitting in the lonely, shady wood,
do you play upon this sweet-voiced reed?
b. That over these dewy mountains my heifers may graze,
plucking the fair-haired ears of corn.
232. Simonides
Me, the goat-footed Pan, the Arcadian, who am against the Medes,
who am with the Athenians, Miltiades set up.
233. Theaetetus
On the same
Wood-walker, lover of trees, husband of mountain-dwelling Echo,
Pan, the watchman, the guardian of the well-horned flock,
Pan the rough-shanked, the much-sowing, who, as a migrant,
ran to the battle of the Assyrian spearmen,
when Miltiades set me up, the Persian-driving comrade in arms,
I stand, the guest-gift of an uncalled alliance.
To others the citadels; but the Mede-slaying Marathon
is shared by me and by the Marathon-fighters.
234. Philodemus
The stone holds three immortals; for the head
clearly reveals Pan the goat-horned,
the breast and belly Heracles, and the rest of the thighs
and the shin fell to the lot of winged-footed Hermes.
You will refuse, stranger, to sacrifice no more; for from your one
victim we three deities have our portion.
235. Apollonides
I am a god of the countryside; why do you pour libations
to me in golden cups, and pour the Italian wine of Bromius,
and bind to the rock the round necks of bulls?
Spare them; I do not delight in such sacrifices.
I am Pan of the hillside, of plain wood, a feaster on lambs,
and a drinker of the earthen cup of new wine.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
236. Peritas
Here upon the dry-stone walls Deinomenes set up
the wakeful Priapus, the guardian of his vegetables.
But, thief, see how I am erect. "This," you ask,
"for the sake of a few vegetables?" Of the few.
237. Tymnes
On the statue of Priapus
I do my Priapic part to everything, even if it is Cronus; I make no distinction
of any thief in any way here beside these garden-beds.
"It is unseemly to say these things for the sake of vegetables and gourds,"
someone will say. It was unseemly; but I say it.
238. Pseudo-Lucianus
For form's sake Eutychides set me here,
this Priapus,
the guardian of dry vine-twigs;
and I have a deep precipice round about me. Whoever comes,
has nothing to steal but me, the guardian.
239. Apollonides
Anaxagoras set me up, the Priapus not upon his feet,
but kneeling on both knees on the ground;
Philomachus made me. But seeing fair Charito near me,
seek no longer how I fell.
240. Philippus
a. The figs look ripe; if you would let me
take a few. b. Touch not a single one.
a. How angry Priapus is! b. You will say more, and go away empty.
a. Yes, I beseech you. b. Give me; for I too am in want.
a. Do you need anything from me, tell me? b. There is some law:
give and take. a. And you, a god, in need of money?
b. I love another thing. a. What is this? b. Eating my own
figs, give me cheerfully the dried fig in return.
241. Marcus Argentarius
I am ripe. I know it too, traveller. No longer praise
the fig, nor look at the bough nearby;
I, Priapus, stand here looking very sharp,
keeping the watch over the figs that befits me.
But if only you touch the fig, you will give a fig in return;
for equality of all is the most just.
242. Erycius
On the same
How heavy, Priapus, and well-knotted, is this weapon,
which you have poured forth, all of it, from your groin,
ready for marriage; and a thirst for women holds you,
my good fellow, and your whole soul swells with longings.
But calm this swollen
member, and hide it beneath a flowery cloak;
for you dwell on no lonely mountain, but beside Helle's
holy shore you tend Lampsacus.
243. Antistius
A field-guard I stand in rich-yielding fields,
saving Phricon's hut and his plants,
saying this to each one: "When you have laughed, seeing me
and my equipment, go your own way.
But if you trespass to what is unlawful, the hairy thing
will be no help to you; we know how to pierce all men."
244. Agathias Scholasticus
On the image of a Satyr holding a pipe to his ear and as if listening
By itself, little Satyr, does your reed send forth sound?
Or why do you bend your ear and lead it to the pipe?
And he, laughing, kept silent; perhaps he would have spoken,
but he was held by the forgetfulness of his delight.
For no wax stopped him; willingly he embraced silence,
turning his whole heart to the business of the pipe.
245. Leontius Minotaurus
Dionysus, seeing the Satyr in such pain,
and pitying him, made him of stone.
But not even so did he cease from his heavy-burdened pains;
for still he toils, even being stone, the wretched one.
246. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Either the Satyr crept beneath the bronze, or by art
the bronze, compelled, was poured around the Satyr.
247. Neilus
On the image of a Satyr made of mosaic in Antioch
a. All Satyrs are mockers; but tell me, you too,
why, looking at each one, do you pour out this laughter?
b. Held by wonder I laugh, how, gathered from stone,
piece by piece from here and there, I suddenly became a Satyr.
248. Plato
Diodorus put the Satyr to sleep, he did not carve him.
If you prod him, you will wake him; the silver holds sleep.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
249. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Beholding this fair image, Aphrodite,
man, propitiate her, sitting near;
and praise Glycera, daughter of Dionysius, who dedicated me
beside the soft wave of the purple shore.
250. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Eros
See how the winged one breaks the winged thunderbolt,
showing that fire is stronger than fire, Eros.
251. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Who fashioned a winged Eros facing the winged Eros?
Nemesis, warding off bow with bow,
that he might suffer what he did; and the bold one, once fearless,
weeps, having tasted the bitter shafts,
and thrice spat into his deep bosom. Ah, a great marvel:
one shall kindle fire with fire; Eros has touched Eros.
252. Anonymous Epigrammatists
I too am of Cypris' blood; my mother bade me
bear bow and wings against my brother.
253. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Artemis
a. Artemis, where is your bow, and the quiver at your neck?
And where the buskin of your Lycastian shoes,
and the brooch wrought of gold, and the purple robe
that winds down to the back of your knee?
b. Those I arm myself with for the hunt; but to the sacrifices
I go just as I am, meeting the holy offerings.
254. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Hermes
A holy heap of stone the passers-by poured up
for me, Hermes; and in return for the little
I felt for them no great gratitude, but only that the rest
of the way to the fountain of Aex I reckon seven stades.
255. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Traveller, do not creep up to the vine-twigs,
nor to the apples, nor where the medlars are;
but there, toward the rushes, pass by,
that you may break nothing of these, nor pluck off
what with toil the planter Midon has won,
who set me here too; and if you do not heed me,
you will know Hermes, how I requite the wicked.
256. Anonymous Epigrammatists
I hold a rugged and lonely spot, traveller;
not I, but Archelochus who set me here is to blame.
For you did not rush as a mountain-lover, nor a hilltop-dweller,
but rather, sir, content with the footpaths.
And Archelochus, being himself a lover of solitude and neighbourless,
O passer-by, set me too to dwell beside him so.
257. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Dionysus
From the fire, O Dionysus, behold, a second time in bronze
you have appeared; Myron has found another birth for you.
258. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Pan
At the fire-offering of Dictynna's shrine the Cretan
set me up in bronze, Pan the goat-hooved.
I have a skin, and a double hare-club; and from a rocky
cave I stretch a double gaze toward the mountain.
259. Anonymous Epigrammatists
From Parian stone the Athenians set me up on the height
of Pallas' city, Pan the trophy-bearer.
260. Anonymous Epigrammatists
If I, Priapus, see you set your feet near the vegetables,
I will strip you bare, thief, on the very garden-bed.
"It is shameful to do this work," you will say; I know it myself, a god;
but I was set up, you should know, for this shameful purpose.
261. Leonidas
By both roads I stand, Priapus, a guardian,
my club raised straight up from my thighs.
For Theocritus set me up to be faithful; but far off
go, thief, lest you weep when you take my vein.
262. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The goat-footed one, who lifts the wine-skin, and the laughing
Nymphs, of Praxiteles, and the fair Danaë.
All of white marble, and the work of supremely skilful hands. Momus himself
will declare: "Father Zeus, this wisdom is unmixed."
263. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Nemesis
Before, a stone, the Persians brought me here, that they might set up
a trophy of victory; but now I am Nemesis.
And I stand for both, a trophy of victory
for the Greeks, and for the Persians the nemesis of the war.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
264. Anonymous Epigrammatists
To Isis the fruit-bearer, mother of the corn-ear, of countless forms,
into the stone basket, far from the toilsome ploughs,
the fruits go of their own accord to their mother.
264a. Anonymous Epigrammatists
To the Nymphs this statue; and the place is their care.
Yes, may it be their care, as the streams of the springs flow undying.
265. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Momus
Who fashioned with blameless hands all-mourning and thrice-wretched
Momus, who grieves over good things?
How, like an old man cast upon the ground, as though living,
he rests from his griefs, his limbs weighed down.
The two-rowed deadly furrow of his teeth reveals it,
gnashing at the good fortunes of his neighbours,
and the shrivelled weight of his frame; with one hand he props
his bare temple, casting it on his aged palm,
and with the other, grinning, he leans his staff against the ground,
dumbly hateful toward the soulless stone.
266. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same
Waste away from your wretched nails, all-devouring Momus,
waste away, gnashing your venom-shooting jaws.
The stretched sinews reveal you, and the veins of your joints,
and the empty, soul-failing strength of your flesh,
and the hair bristling about your shrivelled temples.
. . .
So who by art wrought you, the living bane of a man,
leaving not even room for your biting mouth?
267. Synesius
On the image of Hippocrates
a. Whence is he who set it up? b. A Byzantine. a. And his name?
b. Eusebius. a. And you, who are you? b. Hippocrates of Cos.
a. Why has he painted you? b. For the sake of words: the city to him,
in return for the pencils' work upon me, has given the honour.
a. And why did he not paint his own likeness? b. Because, honouring
us instead of himself, he has the greater glory.
268. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Either Paean painted your voice, Hippocrates,
or you are the witness of his healing art.
269. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This man opened the hidden paths of healing,
the Paean of mortals, Hippocrates of Cos.
270. Magnus
On the image of Galen
There was a time, Galen, when through you the earth
received mortals but reared immortals,
and the halls of much-wept Acheron were widowed,
forced by your healing hand.
271. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Sosander the horse-doctor
Healer of men, Hippocrates, but of horses too,
Sosander, knower of the hidden healing art,
either change your craft, or your name; and let neither
be called from the craft of which the other is master.
272. Leontius Minotaurus
On the image of Iamblichus the physician
Iamblichus, sweet among all, who came to old age
pure of the converse of Cypris;
plying the works of healing, and teaching wisdom,
he never stretched out his hands to unholy gains.
273. Crinagoras
On the image of Praxagoras the physician
The son of Phoebus himself, anointing his hand with the all-healer,
laid upon your breast, Praxagoras,
the grief-soothing knowledge of his art. Therefore all the pains
that arise from long fevers,
and whatever sufficient remedies to lay upon flesh that is cut,
you know from gentle Epione.
If such healers had availed mortals,
the corpse-laden ferry would not have been rowed across.
274. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Oribasius the physician
This great healer of the emperor Julian,
worthy of his piety, divine Oribasius.
For like a bee he had a wise mind, gathering from here and there
the flowers of the physicians of old.
275. Posidippus
On the statue of Opportunity
a. Who and whence is the sculptor? b. From Sicyon. a. And his name?
b. Lysippus. a. And who are you? b. Opportunity, the all-subduer.
a. Why do you walk on tiptoe? b. I am ever running. a. And why have you
winged feet, two of them? b. I fly with the wind.
a. And why do you carry a razor in your right hand? b. A sign to men
that I am sharper than any edge.
a. And your hair, why over your face? b. For him who meets me to seize.
a. By Zeus, and why is the back of your head bald?
b. Because once I have run past on my winged feet,
no one, however he longs, shall catch me from behind.
a. For what reason did the craftsman fashion you? b. For your sake,
stranger; and at the doors he set me as a lesson.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
276. Bianor
Periander set up this image of Arion,
and of the sea-dolphin that swam beside
the perishing man. And the tale tells of Arion:
"We are slain by men, but saved by fishes."
277. Paulus Silentiarius
On the image of a girl harper in Byzantium
The pencil scarcely showed your beauty; would it had power
to make also the sweet melody of your clear-singing mouth,
that in our eyes and ears alike, from your face
and from your lyre-playing, we might be equally charmed.
278. Paulus Silentiarius
On the image of Maria the harp-singer
She has the plectrum of the harp, and she has also the plectrum of love;
and with both she strikes both the heart and the lyre.
Wretched are they whose heart she holds unbending; but on whom she nods,
this one is another Anchises, that one another Adonis.
And if you wish, stranger, to hear her far-famed
name and homeland too: from Pharos, Maria.
279. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the singing stone of the harper in Megara
Remember me, the sounding stone, as you pass by,
the Nisaean; for when Alcathous was building the tower,
then Phoebus lifted on his shoulder the building-stone,
laying down his Lycorean lyre.
Hence I am a lyre-singer; and striking me with a small
pebble, take the proof of my boast.
280. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On a bath
With the wealth of Agathon the people of Tegea
built this bath here, a wonder even for those to come.
281. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On a bath in Prainetus
The present bath was not a bath before,
but a place of refuse, a spot for excrement;
but now it surpasses in splendour the delightful things
that are praised and pleasing to all. For Alexander,
priest of the Nicaeans, a star of glorious wisdom,
built it with his own money and at his own expense.
282. Palladas
We Victories are here, the laughing maidens,
bringing victories to the city that loves good men.
Those who love the city painted us,
stamping us in the forms that befit Victories.
283. Leontius Minotaurus
On the image of a dancing-girl
The tenth of the Muses, Rhodocleia the fourth of the Graces,
the delight of men, the splendour of the city.
Her eye and her wind-swift feet, and the wise fingers
of the Graces, are greater than the Muses and the Graces.
284. Leontius Minotaurus
On the image of another dancing-girl in the Sosthenium
I am Helladia the Byzantine, and here I stood,
where in spring the people hold the dance,
where the land is divided by the strait; for both
shores praised our dancing.
285. Leontius Minotaurus
On the gilded image of a harp-girl
No one cast gold upon Anthousa, but the son of Cronus himself
poured himself about her, as once upon Danaë;
but he did not approach her body, since modesty took hold of his mind,
lest unwillingly he mingle with one of the Muses.
286. Leontius Minotaurus
In the dance the female nature prevails; yield, you youths;
the Muse and Helladia made this law:
the one, because she first invented the rhythms of movement,
the other, because she reached the summit of the art.
287. Leontius Minotaurus
Someone sang of Hector, a new strain; and Helladia,
having put on a cloak, answered to the strain.
And there was longing and dread at the dances of Enyo;
for with manly strength she mingled female grace.
288. Leontius Minotaurus
On the image of Libania the dancing-girl
You have the name of frankincense, the body of the Graces, the ways of Persuasion,
maiden, and the cestus of the Paphian below your flanks.
But in the dances, like nimble Eros, you sport,
drawing all to you by beauty and by art.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
289. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Xenophon of Smyrna
We thought we saw Iobacchus himself, when at the Lenaea
the old man led the young men's dance-frenzy,
and the youthful dances of Cadmus, and the woodland
messenger, the track-following of the joyous revel-bands,
and Agave crying euoi in her son's blood,
raging. Ah, the divine acting of the man!
290. Antipater
On the statue of Pylades the dancer
He put on the reveller-god himself, when he led the Bacchants
from Thebes to the Italian stage,
Pylades, a sweet terror to men, who, dancing
the unmixed deity, filled all the city.
Thebes knows him who came from the fire; but heavenly
is this man, brought to birth by his all-voiced hands.
291. Anyte
To shaggy-haired Pan and the Nymphs of the fold
Theudotus the shepherd set this gift beneath the peak,
because, when greatly wearied by the parching summer,
they refreshed him, holding out honey-sweet water with their hands.
292. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the two books of Homer
Son of Meles, Homer, for you set glory for all Hellas
and for your homeland Colophon for ever,
and you begot these daughters with your godlike soul,
writing two pages from your breast;
the one sings the much-wandering return of Odysseus,
the other the Iliac war of the sons of Dardanus.
293. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Who is he that engraved the war of Troy on his pages,
or who the long wandering of the son of Laertes?
I find no clear name, no city. Heavenly Zeus,
does Homer ever hold the glory of your verses?
294. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Of what homeland shall we record Homer a citizen,
that man, to whom all cities stretch out their hands?
Or is that unknown, and did the hero, equal to the immortals,
leave to the Muses his country and his lineage?
295. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The soil of Smyrna did not bear divine Homer,
nor Colophon, the star of luxurious Ionia,
nor Chios, nor fruitful Egypt, nor holy Cyprus,
nor the rugged island, the home of the son of Laertes,
nor Argos of Danaus, nor Cyclopean Mycenae,
nor the city of the ancient-born sons of Cecrops.
For he was no work of earth; but from the sky the Muses
sent him, that he might bring longed-for gifts to mortals.
296. Antipater
Some say Colophon was your nurse, Homer,
some fair Smyrna, some name Chios,
some Ios, some cried out well-allotted Salamis,
some too Thessaly, mother of the Lapiths;
others proclaimed one nurse, others another. But if I must
declare openly the wise prophecies of Phoebus,
great heaven is your homeland, and from no mortal
mother were you born, but you came of mother Calliope.
297. Anonymous Epigrammatists
