Seven cities contend over the root of Homer:
Cyme, Smyrna, Chios, Colophon, Pylos, Argos, Athens.
298. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Seven cities strove over the wise root of Homer:
Smyrna, Chios, Colophon, Ithaca, Pylos, Argos, Athens.
299. Anonymous Epigrammatists
a. Were you born in Chios? b. I say not. a. What then, of Smyrna? b. I deny it.
a. And is Cyme or Colophon your homeland, Homer?
b. Neither. a. Is Salamis your city? b. Not from her either
was I born. a. But tell yourself where you were born.
b. I will not say. a. Why so? b. I am persuaded that, if I spoke the truth,
I should make the other cities hateful to me.
300. Anonymous Epigrammatists
For ever, Homer, and out of every age you are sung,
having lifted up the glory of the heavenly Muse.
For you sang the wrath of Achilles, you sang the whirling
confusion of the Achaeans' ships upon the sea,
and Odysseus of crafty counsel, worn with his wanderings,
whose bed Penelope gladly beheld.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
301. Anonymous Epigrammatists
If Homer is a god, let him be revered among the immortals;
but if again he is not a god, let him be thought a god.
302. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Nature found him, scarcely found him; and giving him birth she ceased from her toils,
turning her whole effort to Homer alone.
303. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Who is ignorant of the great voice of Homer?
What land, what sea does not know the battle of the Achaeans?
The people of the Cimmerians, deprived of the all-seeing radiance
of the sun, heard the name of Troy; Atlas heard it,
holding the broad-breasted heaven laid upon his shoulders.
304. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Passing through the scorched land, Homer,
you made the unsacked cities envious.
305. Antipater
On the image of Pindar
As much as the trumpet outsounds the bone pipes,
so much above all others did your lyre cry out;
and not in vain did that swarm fashion about your soft lips,
Pindar, the wax-bound honey.
Witness is the Maenalian horned god, who sang a hymn
of yours, and forgot his pastoral reeds.
306. Leonidas
On Anacreon
Behold old Anacreon, soaked deep in wine,
upon the rounded, twisting stone,
how the old man, with moist, lustful eyes,
drags his cloak down even to his ankles;
and of his two shoes he has lost the one, like a drunkard,
but on the other he fits his shrivelled foot.
He sings either of lovely Bathyllus, or of Megistes,
swinging in his hand the lovesick lyre.
But, father Dionysus, guard him; for it is not fitting
that a servant of Bacchus should fall from Bacchus.
307. Leonidas
See how the old man Anacreon, from drink,
is tripped up, and his cloak drags
down to his limbs; and of his slippers the one
he still keeps, but the other he has lost.
And he sings, plucking the tortoise-shell,
of either Bathyllus, or fair Megistes.
Guard the old man, Bacchus, lest he fall.
308. Eugenes
Him who was reared with the honey-sweet Desires,
Lyaeus, Anacreon, the Teian swan,
you tripped with the liquid care of nectar.
For his sidelong glance, and the hem of his cloak cast
about his ankles, and the single
sandal prove his drunkenness; but the lyre even so
gathers up its hymn to the Loves.
Keep the old man from falling, Euius.
309. Anonymous Epigrammatists
You behold me, the Teian, insatiable of both loves,
an old man, equal to boys, equal in pleasing girls;
my eye weighed down with Bromius, and from the revels
the sweet signs of sleepless all-night festivals.
310. Damocharis
On the image of Sappho
Nature the sculptress herself gave you to fashion
the Mytilenean Pierian, O painter.
The clear brightness wells up in her eyes; this plainly
shows an imagination full of well-aimed thought.
The flesh, by itself smooth and not over-wrought,
shows the simplicity she revealed.
And mingled from a cheerful and a thoughtful face,
she announces the Muse joined with Cypris.
311. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the Halieutica of Oppian
Oppian, gathering the sea-faring tribes into his pages,
set before all young men a boundless feast.
312. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Georgius
Queen Calliope, seeing Georgius, said:
"This is my true-born child, not the son of Cronus."
313. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Ptolemy the orator in Antioch
a. Image, who set you up? b. Words. a. Whose are you? b. Ptolemy's.
a. Which one? b. The Cretan's. a. For what? b. In return for virtue.
a. Of what kind? b. Of every kind. a. Toward whom? b. Toward pleaders.
a. And wood suffices? b. Yes; it accepts no gold.
314. Arabius
The city would have given Longinus a golden image,
had not lady Justice turned away the gold.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
315. Thomas
Of rhetoric I love three stars, because they alone
of all orators are the best:
I love your labours, Demosthenes; and I am much
both a lover of Aristides and a lover of Thucydides.
316. Michaelius
On the image of Agathias Scholasticus
The city, admiring the rhythm of the twofold eloquence
of Agathias the orator and verse-singer,
fulfilled, like a mother for her son, and gave this
image, a witness both of love and of wisdom;
and his father Memnonius, and his brother with him,
she set up, tokens of a most reverend lineage.
317. Palladas
Seeing Gessius deaf and voiceless, whether he is stone,
Delian, prophesy: who, or whose, is this stone.
318. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of an untalented orator
Who painted you, the speechless, in the likeness of an orator?
You are silent, you do not speak; nothing is more like.
319. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Marinus the orator
Images are a dear honour for men; but to Marinus
an insult, since the unfitness of his form is exposed.
320. Anonymous Epigrammatists
[On the statue of Aristides the orator
Aristides ended the Ionian
cities' strife,
which before they held over the lineage
of Homer.
For all the cities say: "Smyrna
bore divine Homer,
she who also gave birth to Aristides the orator."
321. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This is the image of Callistus the orator; and you who come
past it, pour libation to Hermes the god of speech.
322. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Phyrmus set up me, Phyrmus, the torch-bearer the torch-bearer,
the son the orator the father the orator.
323. Mesomedes
The workman, having struck off
the glass, carried it;
and into the fire he put the lump,
like strong iron;
and the glass, like wax,
poured itself out, kindled
by the all-devouring flames;
and it was a marvel for mortals to see
the molten stream flowing from the fire,
and the workman trembling,
lest, falling, it should shatter.
And into the points of the double
pincers' jaws he set the lump.
324. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The pencil was silver when I came from the fire and was made,
but in your hands I become golden too.
Thus to you, O graceful Leontion, Athena well
gave the heights of art, and Cypris well of beauty.
325. Julianus
On the statue of Pythagoras
Not the Pythagoras who unfolds the cunning nature of numbers
did the sculptor wish to make,
but the one in prudent silence; and perhaps a voice
he hides within, and is able to bestow even this.
326. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Pythagoras
This is Pythagoras himself, whom the painter, with a voice,
you would have seen, if Pythagoras had wished to speak.
327. Joannes Barbucallus
How wise the painter was; he put no life into the wax,
granting this to the soul of Socrates.
328. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Plato, teaching the mind to walk the upper air,
pours forth the discourses of things beyond the mind.
329. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the image of Aristotle
This is Aristotle, measuring the earth and the vault of the stars.
330. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The mind and the soul of Aristotle; one likeness of both.
331. Agathias Scholasticus
On the image of Plutarch
Your much-famed likeness the sons of the mighty Ausonians
set up, Plutarch of Chaeronea,
because in parallel lives you matched the best of the Greeks
with the warlike dwellers of Rome.
But a life parallel to your life, another,
not even you could write; for you have no equal.
332. Agathias Scholasticus
On the image of Aesop
Well done, old Lysippus, Sicyonian sculptor,
that you set up the likeness of Aesop the Samian
before the Seven Sages; for those laid down compulsion,
not persuasion, in their sayings,
but he, speaking timely things with wise tales and fables,
playing in earnest, persuades men to be prudent.
The rough exhortation is to be shunned; but the Samian's
sweet fable has a fair allurement.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
333. Antiphilus
The wallet and the cloak and the barley-cake soaked in water,
and the staff propped before the feet,
and the cup of earthenware, were enough measures of life
for the wise dog; and even in these there was something more:
for, seeing a peasant draw drink in his hollow hands,
he said: "Why did I in vain burden myself with you, potsherd?"
334. Antiphilus
Even bronze grows old with time; but your glory
all eternity, Diogenes, shall not destroy;
since you alone showed mortals the self-sufficient
fame of life, and the lightest path of living.
Inscriptions on the statues of the athletes in the Hippodrome of Constantinople.
335. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Porphyrius
Porphyrius, son of Calchas, the emperor and the people raise up,
weighed down with many well-earned crowns,
among all charioteers the youngest, yet the best,
who bore off so great a might of victory.
It would have befitted him to stand in a golden statue, not in bronze,
this man, like to the others.
336. Anonymous Epigrammatists
In four ways before, in factions divided, the people cried out,
longing for Porphyrius, son of Calchas; but he,
having placed on the right hand of the royal seat
the reins and the horseman's belt,
from there urging on, drives; and in the midst of his contests
he was set in bronze, with his first down upon his cheek.
And if the prize of years came too swiftly, yet for his victories
it came late, and scarcely, after many crowns.
337. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Cytherea loved Anchises, and Selene Endymion;
and now perhaps Victory loves Porphyrius,
who, ever exchanging his own horses and those of his like-minded
rival, one team for another,
often wreathed his head with day-long contests,
without toiling, his comrade alone following.
338. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This prize, Porphyrius, Victory gave to you a youth,
which time grants to others late and scarcely, when grey;
for, numbering your much-crowned toils,
she found them greater than those of aged charioteers.
What more, since the people of your rivals themselves, shouting,
acclaimed your glory in admiration?
Blessed is the wholly free race of the Blues,
to whom the great emperor nodded that they should have you as a gift.
339. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The valiant the valiant, the wise the wise, the son of Victory,
the children of Victory, Porphyrius, the Blues
set up; for, exchanging his colts on both sides,
he glories in victories, with those he gave and those he took.
340. Anonymous Epigrammatists
To the others when they ceased, but to Porphyrius alone
while still contending, the emperor gave this prize.
For often, having won, he gave his swift horses away,
and took those of his rivals, and was crowned again.
Hence among the Greens was endless strife, hence the cry:
"Who will delight both Blues and Greens, O Lord?"
341. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The votes of all, while I was still driving,
set me, Porphyrius, near to Victory.
For my own people asked the prize; but the others
sought to have me again, renouncing their strife.
And in skill I surpass the charioteers, to whom, offering even horses
better than theirs, I showed them inferior.
342. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Porphyrius himself the sculptor wrought exactly in bronze,
fashioning him as if breathing.
But who shall wrought his grace, his contests, his god-given skill of art,
and his victory never exchanged?
343. Anonymous Epigrammatists
In a bronze image the bronze charioteer
the lord of the Ausonians set up as victor,
as wise, as beloved of the Blues; but for the victories
of Porphyrius we shall see many images.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
344. Anonymous Epigrammatists
a. Who are you, dear youth, with the first edge of beard upon your cheek?
b. Stranger, Porphyrius. a. What is your homeland? b. Libya.
a. And who has honoured you now? b. The emperor, for my horsemanship.
a. Who is the witness? b. The people of the Blues.
a. It would have befitted you to have Lysippus as witness of so great
a victory, Porphyrius, a sculptor of knowledge.
345. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Near to Victory and to King Alexander
you stood, gathering the glories of both.
346. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The eye of Fortune passes over all things; but upon the toils
of Porphyrius alone the eye of Fortune is drawn.
347. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Admiring your rolling whip and your shield, the people
wished to set you up twofold, as was right,
a mighty charioteer and a champion; but the bronze
was not poured in two, fashioning your soul.
348. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Porphyrius the charioteer, for what reason did the people,
who hold the first place, set him up of those they set up?
The emperor himself proclaimed it. What more, that he honours him
for his goodwill, for his horsemanship?
349. Anonymous Epigrammatists
To Porphyrius, after his contests, a prize worthy of his deeds
the lord gave, granting this favour to the Greens.
For often the people, bringing forth more excellent deeds,
praised Calliopas, and again Porphyrius.
This is a double name, which the bronze hero won,
this man, who took the glory of valour with his four-horse teams.
350. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Not only in the race-courses did lady Victory crown you,
but also in wars she showed you a prize-winner,
when the emperor warred, having the Greens as his helpers,
against the savage, raging royal foe,
and the dread tyrant fell, when Rome was perishing then,
and the day of Ausonian freedom came.
Therefore to them the emperor gave their prize, as before they had,
and your likeness art carved, Porphyrius.
351. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The blameless heralds of your contests are
even the crowns from your rivals, Porphyrius.
For all in the race-courses, by turns, you ever confound,
your rival craftsmen, the plaything of your horsemanship.
Therefore you alone have found this strange privilege,
a bronze image among both peoples.
352. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The sculptor made bronze like the charioteer;
would that he had also wrought the mass of his art,
the mass together and the beauty; which Nature, having borne it late,
swore: "I cannot be in labour with it a second time."
She swore beneath truthful lips; for to Porphyrius,
first and alone, she gave all grace.
353. Anonymous Epigrammatists
If envy would be still, and men would judge the contests,
all are witnesses of the toils of Porphyrius;
yes, perhaps they would say, having numbered his contests:
"This is a small prize for so many labours."
For all that ever adorns charioteers, divided,
gathered into one, so great did he appear.
354. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Reverencing you in bronze, thrice-longed-for one, the city honours you;
for it wished gold, but it looked to Nemesis.
And if the right-minded people of the Greens does not cease
singing your customary victory, Porphyrius,
all your statues are breathing; and superfluous
even is gold that comes into rivalry with these.
355. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Not yet, for your toils, did Fortune give you prizes worthy of victory;
for your victories are greater than your good fortune.
But may you abide in the first, steadfast and better place,
melting the envious heart of your enemies,
who, ever seeing your victorious whip,
ever blame their own folly.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
356. Anonymous Epigrammatists
For others the pretext of prizes is time; but those who are judged
by victories do not need grey hair,
but valour, whence boasting is kindled. One among such,
Porphyrius, won the splendour of gifts twice,
boasting not of decades of years, but of hundreds of victories,
many, and all of them kinsfolk of the Graces.
357. Leontius Minotaurus
Cytherea loved Anchises, and Selene Endymion,
so the men of old tell in their tales.
But now a new tale shall be sung, how perhaps Victory
loved the eyes and the chariots of Porphyrius.
358. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Calliopas
While a youth you conquer the elder, and an old man the young,
the goading drivers of prize-winning four-horse teams.
Having completed six decades of years, a statue for your victories
you won, Calliopas, by the nod of the sovereignty,
that your glory might remain even afterwards. Would that for you,
as your glory is immortal, your body too were immortal.
359. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This bronze likeness of your form, Calliopas, of holy
shape, your driver Victory set up,
because, an old man, you conquered the lusty in horse-taming strength,
and the aged you, being young, in skill.
Hence the free-born people of the Blues fixed for you
two prizes, the one of art, the other of strength.
360. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Your old age outran your youth in victories,
and you prevail over all, always, Calliopas.
Hence the emperor and the free people again raise
this prize, a memorial of wisdom and of manhood.
361. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This, theatre-rouser, is your likeness, which the swarm
of conspicuous crowns raises for you, Calliopas.
For neither did a charioteer deceive you, nor with the bridle
did the hard-mouthed horse's jaw disobey your reins.
You alone win the prize of victory. Truly among all
you have the repute of leaving the contests' prizes to others.
362. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Calliopas of famous toils, what more for you, that the emperor honours
your labours with a bronze-wrought image,
the people of countless voices, the whole city? When even
the hand of your enemies itself assented to your toils.
363. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Faustinus
The mind, mother of prizes well won, not the strength of youth,
not the speed of horsemanship, not the season of good fortune.
Be gracious, Faustinus, your mind, which all these things
follow, with which Victory is an immortal companion.
364. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Before, when you were young, Faustinus, the mind of the old feared you;
now, being old, the strength of the young shudders at you.
And second to none did your toil find all things, which honours you
an old man among youths, and among the old a youth.
365. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Constantine
Since Constantine went down within the house of Hades,
the race-course was filled with the gloom of horsemanship,
and delight forsook the spectators; nor in the streets
can those dear contentions be seen.
366. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Your image, Constantine, the citizens set up,
mourning, the delight of their soul being departed.
When the people set the seal of glory upon you, dead,
the emperor too, after your death, remembered your toils;
for which the mocking art of horsemanship perished,
all of it ceasing in you, and having begun in you.
367. Anonymous Epigrammatists
While still you lived, Constantine, the city once
judged a bronze image a small prize;
for all the people knew how many, for the glory of victory,
ever contending, you bound about your head as crowns.
But when you died, longing, it set up this dear likeness of you,
that even for those to come it might keep the memory of your toils.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
368. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The Blues, ever opposed to the Greens,
cried out together to one bound of concord,
that you, Constantine, might receive a funeral boast,
sung by all, pleasing to all.
369. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Of the East and the West, the South and the North
your high-shining course encircles the bounds,
imperishable Constantine. And let no one say you have died;
for not even Hades lays hold of the unconquered.
370. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Near to his own lineage he won this image;
for it befitted three in one to hold a place,
who in the race-courses found a like glory of valour,
taking an equal swarm of countless crowns.
371. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The city set up Constantine, son of Faustinus,
neighbour by lineage, but greater than charioteers.
For long contending he did not fail, but upon a victory
he ceased, having begun before with victory too,
whom, when he was still a boy, the older charioteers,
having crowned in the race-courses, set as judge of the games.
372. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This to you, Constantine, your nurse Victory gave,
following you from childhood through all your years.
For having completed five decades of years in the race-courses,
you found yourself neither equalled nor a little behind.
But even as a boy and beardless you conquered men,
and your equals when grown, and the young when old.
373. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The city wished Constantine to drive forever;
it wished it, but to its longing Nature did not assent.
Hence this his statue found a consolation for their loves,
that forgetfulness and time might not enfold him,
but love might remain for those who long, and emulation for the drivers,
and ornament for the race-courses, and a tale for those to come.
And someone, seeing afterwards lesser charioteers,
shall call blessed the former generation, which saw him.
374. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Twenty-five prizes Constantine alone
took in a single dawn, and exchanged his horses
with his rivals; and taking those whom before he conquered,
with these same he again took twenty-one victories.
Often strife of both factions fell upon the people,
which should have him; and to him they gave the verdict, from two robes.
375. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Awake, Constantine; why do you sleep a bronze sleep?
The people long for your chariots in the race-courses,
and the charioteers, lacking your teaching,
sit most like to orphaned children.
376. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Uranius
Alone excelling among both peoples,
Uranius won glory from both,
while still driving. And the prize came to him first
from the Greens, beside whom he has a neighbouring place.
They too, when he had ceased from the race-course, led him again
to the chariots, mindful of his former victory.
377. Anonymous Epigrammatists
When he had ceased from the race-courses upon a glorious victory,
the emperor again set Uranius
upon the prize-winning chariots, bestowing on the people a favour; for the city
does not long for Uranius apart from contests.
Therefore, driving a second time, both of his last
victory and of his former, it set him up in admiration.
378. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Uranius has Nicaea near, and younger
Rome, of the one being a son, in the other winning glory.
And he conquers on both sides, since he was ambidextrous
both this way and that, to run ahead or to drive past.
Therefore in golden metal too they inscribed him,
in the most glorious of possessions a glorious charioteer.
379. Thomas
On Anastasius
The bold charioteer, forgetful of the chariot's contests,
Anastasius, the ground here holds him lying,
who bound on so many crowns before, as others
of the charioteers have seen days of racing.

title: Greek Anthology
text:
380. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Porphyrius, of the Blue faction
Having mastered every charioteer on earth,
he was fitly raised to run toward the upper air,
Porphyrius, the wonder of the people of the Blues.
For this man, conquering every charioteer on earth,
rises up, that he may run even with the sun.
381. Anonymous Epigrammatists
The first down blooming on him, this Porphyrius,
son of Calchas, drew the Blue reins.
And I am amazed how some hand paints living
horses of his. For if it strike again,
I think, it will run to find victory once more.
382. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Faustinus, of the Green faction
Behold the play of the architect of the building;
for if it had not been roofed with a strong cover,
toward the heavens Faustinus would have risen, running
as though alive with his horses, once the glory of the Greens.
Lift off the roof, and he reaches the upper air.
383. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This is Faustinus, the former charioteer,
whom the people of the Green faction, finding him,
knew nothing at all of defeat in the race.
For he was an old man, as you see; but his strength
was that of some youth, in no way at all defeated.
384. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Constantine, charioteer of the Whites
Constantine, drawing the reins of the White,
if he had not been pent in by the strength of the building,
would have conquered the three, first reaching the upper air.
Without breath you have seen one who runs the air;
art persuades me to behold this man breathing.
385. Anonymous Epigrammatists
Constantine he was; but in the days of old
he drew nimbly the four-horse team of white colour.
But since Charon snatched this man away, the light
of the contest of horse-races set,
and all the delight of the theatre, and the art.
386. Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Julian, charioteer of the Reds
The hand knows how to beget those long since dead.
For Julian too is as strong as of old,
drawing and back-drawing the reins of the Red;
and now, painted, he stands on high with his chariot;
the gesture and the hand remain; give him the turning-post.
387. Anonymous Epigrammatists
This Julian, holding the chariot of the Red,
conquered his opponents in the race.
But if the painter had granted him also the grace of breath,
he is ready, a charioteer once more,
both to come first, and to take even the crown.
388. Julianus
Once, weaving a garland, I found
Eros among the roses;
and gripping him by the wings,
I dipped him into the wine.
And taking him, I drank him down;
and now within my limbs
he tickles me with his wings.
